en: The *Kātyāyanasmṛtisāroddhāra* [on the qualities of a king]:
He should be disciplined, accomplished in the sciences, and endowed with a treasury and valor.
A king should be devoted to Brahmins, disposed toward generosity, and dedicated to truth and righteousness.
Free from arrogance, malice, slander, fickleness, and anger; he is confident yet humble, neither overbearing nor timid, eloquent, and pleasant to behold.

Prosperity attends to the utmost degree that wise man who has his senses under control, who has conquered himself, who wields the rod of punishment against those who deserve it, who acts after careful deliberation, and who is steadfast.
[On the Duties of Kings: Due to an abundance of valor, learning, and wealth, and especially because of their sovereignty,
the minds of kings constantly fall into delusion for these reasons.
Therefore, the mind should always be awakened by the twice-born toward the duty of a king;
one must not transgress the words of the Smṛti, which are supremely purifying and meritorious.
By the power of the sound of the Vedas, even the gods dwelling in heaven rejoice there,
being satisfied by the worship of the twice-born.
Therefore, kings should always perform the worship of the twice-born with great effort;
by that, they shall repeatedly attain the status of Śakra as well as the sovereignty of men again and again.
The superintendent of liquor, fallen from heaven, dwells in the form of a king;
he must constantly perform that by which he may attain the ultimate reality.
Kings who remain established in their own dharma shall attain the state of Śakra;
whereas those who always act contrary to proper conduct dwell in the Avīci hell.
That king who, failing to understand correctly, goes under the sway of anger, will dwell for half a kalpa in a terrible hell; of this there is no doubt.
One should appoint as a minister for deliberating on affairs a Brāhmaṇa who possesses these very qualities, who is devoted to the king, and who upholds his lineage.
Where the ministers, courtiers, and physicians speak only pleasing words,
the king there will swiftly fall away from his kingdom, his dharma, and his happiness.
One should not give way to anger at his words,
for these [words] must always be spoken by them as that which is just and well-established.
Where the king personally oversees legal affairs according to dharma,
there the subjects, following virtuous conduct, shall dwell in happiness.
The constant protection of the subjects, the clearing away of thorns,
and the honoring of the twice-born— for this purpose was the king created.
The king is always considered the lord of the earth, but never of any other property;
for he receives a sixth part of its fruit, and not otherwise.
Because the beings dwell therein, their lordship is proclaimed;
their activity consists of the sixth part of the offerings arising from the causes of both auspicious and inauspicious [deeds].
O lord of men, for that king who acts in this manner having abandoned greed,
sons are born to him, and his kingdom and treasury increase.
For that king who, by unjust means, takes taxes, fines, a share of the grain, and tolls from his kingdom, shall partake of sin.
Having set aside what is stated in the treatises on worldly affairs (arthaśāstra), one should follow what is stated in the treatises on righteousness (dharmaśāstra).
Even if a king is wicked, his kingdom shall not perish,
provided he does not act unjustly against the will of his subjects.
But that king who, without affliction, properly presents [the gift] to one who requests it, saves an infinite number of beings; such is the gift for the sake of Dharma.
That which is acquired by kings after conquering an enemy through lawful means is pure; that should be given away, for it has never been offered in any other way.
The king should appoint as his domestic priest a Brahmin who is learned,
well-disposed toward him, accomplished in Vedic study, free from greed, and truthful in speech.
In the extensive exposition of logic (*nyāya*) known as *dharma*, which is to be accomplished through effort and is characterized by [the nature of] legal procedure (*vyavahāra*),
that debate which has the object of proof as its basis is called "legal dispute" (*vyavahāra*).
In the sense of "diversity" (vi) and "doubt" (nānārtha), *hāra* is said to mean "removal";
because it removes diverse doubts, it is traditionally known as *vyavahāra*.
A king, however, should not personally conduct the legal affairs of men who are not disputing, whether out of a desire for power or again, out of greed for wealth.
He who commits violence or does not give what is to be given, or who,
when asked, says "bring it," should be dragged away from his misconduct by order of the king.
When the two lines reach eighteen words due to the distinctions among the objects to be accomplished (*sādhya*),
they become eighteen thousandfold through the distinctions among the ritual actions (*kriyā*).
The root of the doctrine of what is to be proven (sādhyavāda) is that which has been presented by the proponent;
"non-delivery of what is to be given" and "violence" are said to be the two grounds for its emergence.
The plaint, the reply, the rejoinder, and the stage of proof— by these it is declared to have four feet.
In the treatises on Dharma and Artha, however, two branches are proclaimed;
victory and decisive settlement are declared to be the two fruits.
But he who, though urged by the king, first reports a matter condemned by the scriptures— being primarily concerned with his own wealth— is declared to be a *stobhaka* (a defamer).
One who is appointed by the king himself to examine defects in titles,
and having learned of them, reports them to the king, is designated as a "sūcaka" (informant).
[The consideration of the relative strength and weakness of legal procedures, customary conduct, royal edicts, and so forth:
But where, in a dispute, the wrongdoer would have to assume the role of the defendant while the owner of the property would recover his own wealth, that decision is made by the law alone. // K_035 //
Whatever Smṛti scripture has been proclaimed by those who establish Dharma for the purpose of deciding legal cases is indeed known as Vyavahāra.
Whatever is practiced by someone, whether it be righteous or unrighteous,
that which is constantly observed due to the customs of a region is proclaimed as *caritra*.
Whatever law the king establishes in accordance with the treatises on logic (nyāyaśāstra), as well as local custom,
that righteous decree is the royal edict.
But where a matter is consistent with reason and devoid of divine proof,
there dharma is overridden by legal procedure (vyavahāra), and not otherwise.

Regarding those born in the inverse order of castes and those dwelling in outcaste communities, they say that their practice is necessarily contrary [to the norm]; one should not disturb that established custom.
But when the king should issue a final decision according to that dharma,
then the legal proceeding is superseded by that very custom.
But when a legal practice established by kings is contrary to logic,
such a practice should be set aside by the king's command.
Whatever subsequent sublation is joined with this method,
where there is sublation by another means, there dharma is destroyed.
When one's own word exists, self-willed action leads away from heaven, brings about the destruction of the world, causes fear to enemy armies, and robs kings of their life-span and progeny.
Therefore, the king should settle legal matters in accordance with the scriptures;
however, in the absence of scriptural texts for all cases, he should decide them according to local custom.
Whatever custom has been established in a particular region and persists for all time,
provided it does not contradict the Śruti and Smṛti, that is called a "local practice" (deśadṛṣṭa).
For those residing in districts, ports, cattle-pens, cities, or villages,
[the king shall decide] according to their own conventions, or according to the Dharmaśāstras, and for others, together with them.
The settlement that has been determined with the consent of the country must always be recorded in writing and kept sealed with the royal seal.
Having examined it, one should decide [the case] after protecting it with care according to the treatises;
however, whatever matter has been committed to writing and established by those who abide by the scriptures (naigama) [shall be followed].
Therefore, that [cognition] should proceed from that [object]; it should not proceed otherwise.
But that which is seen in a particular place by means of a valid cognition is determined to be "thus."
Where an unprecedented act has been performed that is approved by the Śruti and Smṛti, it should not be done otherwise; one should avoid what is devoid of justice.

[The Court of Justice]: That place where the investigation of the treatises on dharma and the discernment of the root and the essence are carried out is indeed the Court of Justice (dharmādhikaraṇa). K_052 //
Having risen early in the morning and performed his purification with a concentrated mind, the king [should honor] his guru, the astrologer, physicians, deities, Brahmins, and domestic priests.
Having honored these as is appropriate with fine flowers, ornaments, and garments,
and having paid homage to his teachers and others, he should enter the assembly hall with a cheerful countenance.
Having entered the assembly hall with modest attire and composed mind, the king,
seated and facing the east, should attend to the legal affairs of the litigants together with those aged in the three Vedas and with ministers skilled in counsel.
Accompanied by the chief justice, his ministers, the Brahmins and the domestic chaplain, and the members of the assembly, the king remains in heaven as a witness through his adherence to dharma.
Together with his councilors— steadfast, disciplined, wise, hereditary, and the best among the twice-born—
who were skilled in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras and proficient in the Arthaśāstra.
It should be presided over by a few merchants who possess noble lineage, good conduct, age, virtuous behavior, and wealth, and who are free from envy, acting as true members of the community.
In that regard, the listeners should be like merchants who perceive what is right.
[The Time for Seeing Legal Cases: In the assembly halls during the forenoon, the king, the subduer of enemies, shall decide legal cases according to the path laid down by the scriptures.
Except for the eighth part of the day, the three periods of time that remain are declared by the scriptures to be the supreme time for legal proceedings.
The period of time that follows the third of the eight divisions of the first day is seen by the wise in the treatises as the proper time for legal proceedings.
[The Judge]: When the king himself does not perform the adjudication of legal cases,
then he should appoint there a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the scriptures.
One who is capable, of noble birth, impartial, not causing agitation, steady,
fearful of the hereafter, most righteous, diligent, and free from anger.
One who is gentle, sweet-natured, affectionate, patient, discerning,
energetic, and free from greed should be employed by the king in the conduct of debate.
One who studies only a single treatise cannot know how to reach a definitive conclusion regarding legal matters;
therefore, kings should ensure that those most proficient in many traditional sciences are employed in judicial disputes.
Where, however, there is no Brāhmaṇa, one should appoint a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; but one should avoid a Śūdra with every effort.

Therefore, whatever task has been performed by others in an unjust manner should be recognized as such, even if it was carried out by those appointed [to the office], whether by chance or according to the scriptures.
The established rule is that he asks the question concerning the legal dispute *prāk* (first);
therefore, he who investigates that matter is traditionally known as the *prāḍvivāka*.
But if the judge should converse in secret with a litigant regarding a matter that has not yet been decided,
he shall be punished, and the members of the court all the more so.

[The members of the assembly: "The members of the assembly should be the best of the twice-born, free from greed, wealthy, knowers of the Dharma, speakers of truth, and proficient in all the scriptures. K_071.

Where the members of the court have reached a decision by overstepping the science of logic (*nyāyaśāstra*), there dharma, being struck down by adharma, destroys [the wrongdoer]; of this there is no doubt.
Where righteousness is slain by unrighteousness, and truth by falsehood,
while the members of the assembly look on, there the judges themselves are slain.
But the members of the court must not overlook that which proceeds contrary to the law;
for by overlooking it, they, along with the king, go headlong into hell.
Those members of the assembly who follow him even as he proceeds by unjust means share in that guilt;
therefore, they must instruct that king.

But having recognized that the king's mind has strayed from the path of justice, one should speak what is pleasing to him in that situation; such a person, being a member of the assembly, shall not incur guilt.
A member of the assembly must necessarily speak words consistent with dharma and artha;
if the king does not listen, then that member of the assembly is indeed blameless.
When the king directs a dispute toward unrighteousness, the member of the court,
having informed the monarch, should then set aside that case.
Whether out of affection, ignorance, greed, or even delusion, if a member of the assembly speaks otherwise [than the truth], he is to be punished; for he is considered non-member (asabhya).
Having correctly understood the determination of the case, the member of the court should then speak;
otherwise, he must not speak at all, for the speaker shall be subject to a double fine.
But that which has been lost due to the fault of the court members must then be restored by those members;
however, once the matter of the litigants has been definitively settled, one must not overturn it.
[The relative weight of the decision-makers:
Families, guilds, assemblies, and the authorized king are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding. K.082.
But the affairs of ascetics should be carried out by those learned in the three Vedas alone,
and likewise by those who know the application of illusion (māyā-yoga), and not by him personally, for fear of provoking their anger.
One endowed with perfect knowledge should not offer instruction to those of superior birth and character, nor to gurus, teachers, or ascetics.

But that which is their abiding in the lineage, which comes about gradually through the nature of reality (dharmatā), they call the "family dharma" (kuladharma); one should protect it in that very same way.

[The Manner of Inquiry: At the appropriate time, he should question the petitioner who stands before him with a prostration: "What is your business? What is your affliction? Do not fear; speak, O man! (K.086)
"By whom, toward whom, when, and for what reason should one ask? Thus should a member of the assembly inquire.
When asked thus, whatever that Brahmin may say, the members of the assembly should accept it together."
Having deliberated upon the matter, if it is found to be just, he should thereafter summon [the defendant] for that purpose,
or else deposit a seal thereon, or appoint a person to represent him.
One who is presented by the plaintiff as another representative before the judicial authority is to be known as a *pratinidhi* (proxy);
likewise, one who himself accepts the role of the defendant (*prativādī*) is also so designated.
The right [to sue] belongs to the one who is formally accused, not to anyone else, as there would be no logical connection;
yet even the other is considered to have been made an opponent by the one who is accused.
Whether commissioned by the plaintiff or sent by the defendant,
whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory and defeat belong to those two [parties].
Slaves, laborers, disciples, appointed officials, and likewise kinsmen who act as advocates shall not be subject to punishment; however, anyone other than these is liable to a fine.
In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher's wife,
and other such extreme sins, no counter-argument is permitted.
In the case of killing a human, theft, violating another's wife,
eating forbidden food, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden.
In cases of harsh speech, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, no opposing witness shall be permitted;
the perpetrator himself must plead the case.

The king should summon those who are eager for the Dharma, those seeking prosperity, and even the sick or the dull-witted; however, he should not summon those who are mentally unwell, the intoxicated, the insane, the afflicted, or women.
A young woman born of noble family who has not yet reached her menses,
as well as a maiden who is the best among all castes and has already given birth— these are declared to have their kinsmen as masters.
The summoning of those women who are dependent on their families, those who are wanton, prostitutes, those who have lost their kin, and those who are outcastes is prescribed.
One who speaks in debate while armed, without an upper garment, with disheveled hair, seated upon a throne,
or with the left hand [holding a weapon] shall incur punishment.
But if one who is capable should, when summoned, disregard the king's command,
the king shall inflict upon him punishment according to the procedure prescribed by law.
For minor offenses, the fine shall be fifty; for middling offenses, it shall be no less than two hundred;
and for serious matters, the punishment shall always be no less than five hundred.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed for a particular offense, that fine shall be collected from the offender, or its equivalent value shall be paid to the king with due effort.
One who commits violence or fails to pay what is owed should be arrested by the king's command upon being summoned, due to his misconduct.
But once the matter has been reported to the king and he has given an unambiguous promise [to hear it],
one should then apply the injunction of restraint until the appearance for summons.
One who is fit for restraint but has not been restrained deserves punishment upon departing.
[Those who are not to be obstructed:

But he who, by means of restraining the senses, or by means of speech, breathing, and so forth, should obstruct one who ought not to be obstructed— he is to be punished, for he has committed a transgression.
Those who have climbed trees or mountains, those situated on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats,
and all those in difficult terrain— none of these should be obstructed by those seeking to accomplish their purpose.
Those afflicted by disease, those in distress, as well as sacrificers,
those who have not yet crossed over [to the other side], and likewise those who are intoxicated, insane, or mentally dull, are not to be obstructed.
A farmer does not [reap] at the time of sowing, nor does a soldier at the time of marching;
having made a promise and set out, one does not turn back midway once the appointed time has arrived.

A farmer diligently engaged in his crops, from the commencement of work until the arrival of water, shall not be sued during that time; however, it is the established rule that one who restrains a person who should not be restrained shall be punished by the king.
One who is accused, one who is imprisoned, and one who remains under the king's command—
these, the wise know, must not have another person act on their behalf when they themselves are the accused.
Having accomplished the task for the messenger— considering whether it requires one day, two days, or more, and depending on the place, time, and other factors— one should cause him to be given food.
Those who know the truth understand that eating is prescribed everywhere as being dependent upon place, time, age, strength, and so forth, for one who is the agent of action.
[They are not to be accepted as witnesses: neither an owner nor an enemy, nor one appointed by the owner;
likewise, one who has been imprisoned or fined, and those involved in a legal dispute, are never [admissible].
Neither an heir nor one who has been disinherited, nor those who dwell in perpetual residence, nor men appointed to royal service, nor those who have gone forth as renunciants; K_115.
One who is incapable of paying the debt to the creditor and an equivalent fine to the king,
or one whose father is still living and acts according to his own will,
should not be accepted as a surety for the performance of the obligation without being fully examined.
If, however, there is no surety for the plaintiff who is fit to bring the suit,
he, being protected, shall at the end of the day give a fee to the messenger.
A twice-born man who lacks a surety should be protected by those who patrol the outskirts;
however, Śūdras and others who lack a surety should be bound with fetters.
If he transgresses or departs, he should be fined eight paṇas;
however, the obstruction of the daily rites of all social classes must be prevented.
According to the principle of not grasping what has already been grasped, the king should not initiate legal proceedings;
rather, he should either hand over the case to that person or entrust it to another.
[The Order of Speech for the Plaintiff and Others:
In that regard, the plaintiff should speak first, and the defendant immediately thereafter;
at the conclusion of those two, the members of the assembly shall speak, and after that, the presiding judge.
He for whom there is greater suffering or for whom the matter to be proved is more significant shall be the plaintiff;
it is not he who first reports the case who becomes the plaintiff.

If a person suffers a loss concerning their property or experiences significant physical affliction, the right to speak as a plaintiff (arthivāda) should be granted to them; it shall not be given to one who does not report it first.
[The nature of the formal proposition:
Having established the time, the year, the month, the fortnight, as well as the day, the hour, the location, the subject matter, the place, the caste, the appearance, and the age. K. 124.
He should [inform the king] of the matter to be proved, the means of proof, the substance, the number, his own name,
the names of the kings in their proper order, the place of residence, and the name of the person against whom the case is brought.
Having proclaimed the name of the ancestral lineages in due order, as well as the affliction, the acquirer, and the donor,
one should determine the other signs of forgiveness and the specific side [of the claim].
The country, as well as the location, the settlement, the caste, the name, the residence, the measurement, and the name of the field.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should cause these ten things to be recorded: the names of the ancestors and grandfathers, and the eulogies of former kings.
If one should state that [the opponent] has been provoked by even one [of the faults] such as passion (rāga) during the formal procedure,
then one should write "om" for all of it upon the board or other materials of the disputant.
One should rectify matters that are excessive and supplement those that are deficient;
one should establish them upon the ground for as long as the case remains settled.
The judge shall cause the plaintiff’s statement, as it was naturally expressed, to be recorded on a wooden board with chalk;
thereafter, once it has been refined, it shall be written upon a leaf.
A righteous king should punish like a thief anyone who writes down one thing while stating something else in the words of the plaintiff or the defendant.
He may obtain a period of relaxation for three days or even seven days,
as long as the thought arises in him when he wishes to speak in a dispute.
Since a definitive conclusion is reached only after a long time from the commencement of an undertaking,
one who is diligent does not waste time, but rather possesses the proper timing.
In a dispute where the minds of two parties desiring to settle their business do not reach an agreement,
a period of time should be granted to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
[The faults of the proposition:
the faults of the prima facie case] That which is contrary to the state and that which is rejected by the king;
A prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) that is confused by multiple points does not succeed.
Even a case involving many assertions that has been decided in legal proceedings,
the king may, if he desires to ascertain the truth, take it up again at his pleasure.
A thesis that is devoid of place and time, lacking the substance and number [of the probandum], and deficient in the measure of what is to be proven, is considered unacceptable.
If he does not wish to act in accordance with justice, or if he acts unjustly,
or if he fails to have it recorded in writing, his case shall not succeed.
One should avoid a fallacious thesis (pakṣābhāsa) that is unestablished, unassailable, meaningless, purposeless,
impossible to prove, or contradictory.

Those who know the thesis understand the *pakṣa* (the subject) to be that which is free from defects of the proposition, is yet to be proven, is endowed with valid reasons, is certain, and is established in the world.
It consists of very few syllables yet contains abundant meaning; it is free from ambiguity and confusion;
it is devoid of contradictory causes and serves as a refutation of opposing views.
But when such a thesis has been formulated by the proponent,
the opponent should then provide a response connected to that very thesis.
When a claimant states a matter and it is not contested,
or when one remains silent at the time of the gift, that matter is deemed approved.
[The reply should be given either immediately or after a period of time.
Having heard the matter set forth in writing, if the defendant requests a delay in the lawsuit for a valid reason, it should be granted to him without a doubt.

Depending on the gravity or lightness of the matter, such as debts and so forth, he may obtain [the result] immediately, or after one day, five days, or three days; or after three fortnights, or after seven days.
Having ascertained the time, the capacity [of the parties], and the relative strength or weakness of the matters at issue,
the sovereign should grant the defendant either a short or a long period of time.
Whether it be a day, half a month, a full month, a season, or even a year—
the time for repayment by the other party must correspond to the nature of the transaction and its established duration.
Where dignity departs, or where there is destruction or even abandonment, one should not wait for the appointed time; for that matter is indeed urgent.
In the case of a cow, a bull, a field, women, and likewise in procreation; in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, as well as in buying and selling.
In cases of defiling a maiden, theft, quarrel, acts of violence, embezzlement of a deposit, fraud, and perjury, one should initiate a lawsuit immediately.
Bṛhaspati states that in cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, false accusation regarding a cow, and likewise in matters of urgency, one may litigate over land even out of season.
In matters that have been recently committed, the lord should institute a lawsuit immediately;
or, in cases where time has elapsed, he should grant a period of time to the defendant.
In the case of an immediate birth, the impurity lasts for that very day; if it has passed a month, it shall be one day;
if six years have passed, it shall be three nights; and if twelve years have passed, it shall be seven days.
In the twentieth year, he shall receive ten days or half a month;
when thirty years have passed, it shall be one month; and beyond that, it shall be three fortnights.
One may perform it at any time before a year has passed, according to one's own desire;
however, for those who are dull-witted, insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by disease, [the period] is one year.
Or when the matter has reached another region, or when the object is unknown, or when the root witnesses or the witnesses themselves are situated in a foreign land; K_157 //
In that case, the time for men [to pay] would be until their return to their own country;
even when a time has been granted, it may still be paid sooner due to the importance of the matter.
But immediately after that, the defendant, having heard the meaning of the plaintiff's case,
should present his counter-argument connected to the matter of the plaintiff's claim.
In matters concerning conduct, the giving of goods, sacrifices, duties, and attendance,
one should not take advantage when someone is unable to attend.
If at that time there should be a defect caused by fate or the king,
he shall not be defeated merely because his claim is obstructed.
One should establish a fault caused by a king or by fate through witnesses;
however, for one who acts with deceit, that wealth shall be made to pay as a fine.
One who is being prosecuted should never prosecute the prosecutor in return,
except in cases of assault, theft, adultery, and crimes involving mortal sin.
In whatever matter there exists a custom handed down through a traditional succession,
the king, having examined it, shall cause a reply to be given according to that rule.
[The fourfold reply:
The true reply, the false reply, likewise the counter-attack,
and the application of a prior legal decision— thus the reply is of four kinds.
But when another, having heard the meaning of what was spoken, refutes it either in terms of its meaning or its words, that reply should be known as false.
If a defendant, when being charged, should practice concealment of the accusation,
one should know that his defense in the legal proceeding is false.
The truthful speech of one who is to be converted is declared to be "acceptance."
"This is false; I do not know it; I was not present there at that time;
and I was unborn at that time"—thus, falsehood is fourfold.
If the defendant admits the very claim that has been stated by the plaintiff,
the Teacher (Guru) declared that one should state the reason for the reduction [of the fine].
If one who has been defeated according to the formal procedure is made to write again,
he is said to be "previously defeated," and that is called *prāṅnyāya*.
I shall establish [the truth] by means of witnesses, family members, or a written document;
furthermore, this threefold prior claim has already been defeated by me.
[The fallacies of the rejoinder (uttarābhāsa) or the defects of the rejoinder (uttaradoṣa) are: that which is unestablished, contradictory, too little, or excessive;
that which is doubtful, impossible, unclear, or has a different meaning—these are exceedingly defective.
An answer that is non-comprehensive, contains disjointed words, has a hidden meaning, is confused,
requires interpretation, or is substanceless is not praised by the wise.

An answer that consists of disjointed words, is non-comprehensive, has a hidden meaning, is likewise confused, requires interpretation to be understood, or is devoid of substance, does not lead to the accomplishment of one's own purpose.
If, however, one does not understand the convention of the thousand signs and forms,
or if it is stated in another language, that answer is considered unestablished.
"I returned it in my youth; indeed, I did not return it"—when one says this, that contradictory reply should be understood as a *viruddha* (contradictory) rejoinder here.
To say, "This was previously defeated by me for this purpose," or "This was [defeated] by me previously"— that which begins with "by me" is known as an inferior rejoinder (ūna-uttara).
When it should have been said, "It was taken," he instead said, "The task was performed by me;
that wealth which was previously taken was indeed very abundant."
When one ought to say "it must be given by me," saying instead "it is not to be given by me"—
the wise should then recognize such an answer as ambiguous in legal proceedings.
In the past, this [doctrine] was established by force;
they consider this unspoken point to have been stated for some other purpose.
When it is said, "I have given this thousand together with myself," that which is returned as half of that is considered here to be non-pervasive (avyāpaka).
As long as the proponent has not properly established his case,
it is said that what was previously accepted by him is now a "disordered statement."
How could anyone give a lotus that has not been taken?
That answer was stated with a hidden meaning according to conventional usage.
"Should that very same thing always be given, or should it be given by me?"—
those who know the truth understand that this reply is improper.
The reply, "A crow has no teeth," or "It does have them," and so forth, is considered by its very nature to be without substance; therefore, it is not accepted as a correct answer.
One should not overstep what is relevant, the subtle, the unmanifest, the deficient or excessive, the incoherent, the non-pervasive, the essence-less, the doubtful, or that which is opposed.
Any other [reply] that is doubtful, too little compared to the subject matter, or excessive,
as well as that which pervades only a part of the opponent's position (pakṣaikadeśavyāpin), cannot be a valid rejoinder (uttara) at all.
That which is true in one part of the thesis, but constitutes a reason in another part,
and is false in yet another part, is not a valid rejoinder because of its internal inconsistency.
In a single dispute, there should not be a means of proof for both disputants;
for there can be no establishment of the object for both, nor can there be two means of proof in one place.

If, having resorted to grounds that cause the defeat of an argument, one should state another, more significant reason found in the opponent's statement, then indeed that [latter] is what is established, and not the other.
One should give a truthful answer and cause the debtor to pay what they owe by means of conciliation,
sowing dissension, and other such methods, until that matter has been fully resolved.
Whether out of delusion or through deceit, whatever was not stated by the proponent,
even if it is included within the reply, that should be accepted by both parties as well.
But he who, though being urged by various means, does not give an answer,
is considered defeated once seven nights have passed and must pay the debt.
Having caused [the opponent] to hear [his case], he may abandon what ought to be done and state something else;
because he has thereby resorted to another position, that proponent is defeated.
One should not speak of a matter that has not been stated by oneself; nor should one speak after having instigated another.
One who speaks falsely in this manner should likewise be declared defeated.
But if a litigant, having had a statement written down, should then speak of it as being either deficient or excessive, he shall suffer defeat; he does not deserve to maintain his accusation.
The wise should understand that the members of the court and the witnesses constitute the "action" (kriyā);
he who, out of delusion, hates that action is called a hater of the action (kriyādveṣī).
Through failure to attend when summoned, one is immediately cast out.
Even if prepared, one should not speak; otherwise, one deserves immediate imprisonment.
On the second day, one should know that the defeat of that evil-minded person is certain.
But when one seeks to prolong the debate through mere pretext,
one should recognize that as "prevarication" (sāpadeśa), which is recorded as causing the defeat of the argument.
One who speaks falsely shall pay five paṇas; one who shows malice toward the legal proceeding, ten paṇas;
one who fails to appear, twelve paṇas;
one who remains silent when questioned, sixteen paṇas; and one who flees after being summoned shall be made to pay twenty paṇas.
The king should punish one who does not come when summoned three times, one who flees upon being summoned, or one who has exceeded a period of five nights.
If one should divide even one of the legal matters that have been set forth,
and should likewise entice the plaintiff with greed, one should declare him to be defeated.
If he causes fear, or division, or intimidation, or obstruction,
he loses his case in the legal proceeding regarding the matter of the two disputants.
Once the defendant has been summoned in accordance with the fault and the retrial is no longer possible,
and both have committed their written statements and the determination of the case has begun,
whoever speaks what is improper therein shall be defeated on that point.
But that plaintiff who, having pointed out witnesses, does not proceed to litigate by choice,
is defeated after thirty nights have passed.
A debate is accepted for one who is inferior because of fleeing from it or because of resorting to another position, but not for one who has been defeated by his own words.
The wise know that one who has been defeated by an inferior argument may be rescued;
however, for one who is himself deficient in his own argument, no rescue exists.
Those who, having made their claims known, reach a settlement with one another after having already accepted their case,
shall all be fined double, for they have deceived the king.
[The Section on Action (Kriyāpāda):
For even the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) attains the status of a conclusion (uttara) by virtue of its cause;
therefore, action is then said to be that which establishes the prima facie argument.
When the answer has been properly examined and written down as being faultless,
the performance of the legal action is required by either the defendant or the plaintiff.
That which the proponent clearly intends to establish for himself is the "probandum" (sādhya); that by means of which the entire probandum is established is the "proof" (sādhana).
[The Means of Proof, and the Consideration of Their Relative Strength]:
They know that the means of proof are threefold: written documents, witnesses, and possession.
Logical reasoning consists of circumstantial indications, while ordeals here include poison and the like.
Even when the prior claim has been written down in its entirety, letter by letter,
the plaintiff shall establish it in the third stage by means of evidence.
For it has been stated that the "effect" (kārya) is that which is to be accomplished, while the "means" (sādhana) is called the action (kriyā).
That [action], moreover, should be known as twofold: divine (daivikī) and likewise human (mānuṣī).
Human means consist of documents, witnesses, and so forth; divine means are considered to be [the methods of] execution and the like.
When witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid divine means of proof;
for by employing divine means when witnesses are available, he is defeated thereby.
If one person should state human evidence and another should state divine evidence,
the king should accept the human evidence in that case, but not the divine procedure.
If even a human action that pervades only a single part were to exist, it should be accepted by men who speak; however, even one that is complete, if it is divine, is not to be accepted.
The divine [oblation] is of five kinds, while the human is traditionally held to be of three kinds.
He who, setting aside a strong means of proof, relies instead upon a weak one,
shall not obtain that means of proof again once the victory has been determined by the members of the court.
One should abandon that action which, setting aside the essential point, accomplishes many non-essential things and is devoid of substance;
one should avoid from afar that action which attempts to accomplish two opposing sides.
When witnesses are available and when there is a written document, judicial action is not declared to be dependent on fate; in such disputes, neither divine ordeals nor witnesses are required.

A document loses its validity through the lapse of time and likewise by being vitiated according to legal principles. In a dispute lacking documentary evidence or witnesses, one should assign divine means [of proof].
One should not employ human means or a document in a matter that must be settled by divine means.
Regarding the status that has been proclaimed for guilds, corporations, assemblies, and the like, their proof consists of documentary evidence; neither ordeal nor witnesses are required.
Likewise, in matters such as gates, paths, works, enjoyment, and water-conduits, possession alone shall be the weighty proof;
neither documentary evidence nor witnesses [are required].

Furthermore, when a dispute arises between a master and his servants regarding what has been given or not given, or concerning the connection of sale and purchase, one who, having bought, does not deliver the wealth; K_227.
In matters of gambling, challenges, and disputes that have arisen, witnesses are declared the means of proof; neither an ordeal nor a written document is required.
In cases of assault, verbal abuse, physical violence, or threats involving the rod,
as well as in matters arising from the use of force, witnesses or even divine ordeals may be employed.
But for those who commit secret acts of violence, examination by means of ordeals is appropriate,
as well as [examination] through reasoning, signs, gestures, facial expressions, speech, eyes, and behavior of men.
And in all cases involving the highest degrees of violence,
Bhṛgu says that one should determine the true state of affairs by means of divine ordeals when there are no witnesses present.
Where there is equality among witnesses, one should purify the matter even by means of ordeals;
but in disputes where the penalty involves the loss of life, if witnesses are available and the litigant resorts to an ordeal,
one should not question the witnesses in that case.
For a debt, documentary evidence, witnesses, or even a trace of circumstantial reasoning,
or divine proof (ordeals) has been declared as legal procedure for subjects out of a desire for their welfare.
An accusation at the proper time, a fragment of logical reasoning, and likewise a third means, an oath— by these one should recover a debt in due order.
Even if he is urged repeatedly, he should not reject those words;
rather, after three, four, or five times, he should act according to the purpose.
But when there is an objection or contradiction, one should provide a supporting argument through a few logical reasons,
such as those concerning place, time, the relation of objects, measure, action, and so forth.
Even when arguments are insufficient, one should determine the truth by means of oaths alone—
such as those involving fire, water, or meritorious deeds— which take into account the nature of the matter, the time, and the relative strength of the parties.
Where there may be a document involving fraud, if it has been presented to the king,
the king, seated upon the seat of justice, shall have it cleared by means of an ordeal.
In cases of verbal abuse and regarding land, one should not employ divine ordeal.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should administer ordeals;
however, one should establish the matter through witnesses, documentary evidence, and possession.
In all disputes whatsoever, the lord of men should always reach a definitive conclusion by means of authoritative proofs, by logical reasoning, or even through divine evidence.
A written document, witnesses, and possession are remembered as the threefold means of proof;
the wise know inference to be the logical reason, as well as reasoning itself.
In the absence of the preceding [means of proof], one should proceed by the subsequent ones alone, and never otherwise— namely,
by the means of proof (pramāṇas) indicated by the disputant, such as possession, documents, and witnesses.
No one should employ the accuser in the divine ordeals;
those expert in the divine ordeals should administer the ordeal to the accused.

In the case of a false statement, that [burden of proof] shall consist of four parts; likewise in the case of a counter-attack (pratyavaskandana) and in a plea of prior judgment (prāṅnyāya). It should be understood as consisting of two parts in cases of admission (saṃpratipatti).
Defeat is said to be of two kinds: that declared by another and that declared by oneself.
That declared by another is of ten types, while that declared by oneself is recorded as being of one type.
The shifting of the dispute to another matter, contradiction between what precedes and what follows,
the refutation [of one's own position] arising from one's own actions, and the supporting of the opponent's argument— [these are fallacies].
The non-indication of a place, the indication of non-places and non-times, the instigation of witnesses, and the subversion of testimony.
A written document is said to be of two kinds: that executed by one's own hand and that executed by another;
likewise, it may be without witnesses or with witnesses, and its validity depends upon the established customs of the region.
A document written by the debtor’s own hand, accompanied by witnesses, is to be known as a "handwritten document" (svahastalekhya); it is considered authoritative by the wise.
One should record the date of birth, the caste, and the amount of wealth;
for one who acts in this manner, even if the matter is not recorded, it will be remembered and the claimant's cause shall not perish.
A document, however, should be executed with witnesses, with the sequence of its letters uncorrupted,
conforming to the established customs of the region, and complete in all its particulars regarding every matter.

A document that is endowed with proper color, phrasing, and action; that is free from doubt and has clear syllables; and whose sequence and marks are not deficient—such a document shall attain validity.
The status of the four classes of knowledge-holders, guilds, corporations, citizens, and so forth,
as well as any written document intended for the purpose of establishing that status, shall constitute a *sthitipatraka* (a deed of status).
When the curse has been lifted and the penance has been performed by the people,
a certificate of purification should be obtained from them, accompanied by witnesses.
When all the highest forms of imprecation have been invoked,
that written record which recounts the events is to be known as a *sandhipatra* (a treaty document).
When a dispute over boundaries has been settled, a formal boundary document is prescribed.
A document bearing the king's own hand and marked with his seal,
containing witnesses for all matters, is known as a royal edict.
The statements of the plaintiff and the defendant, the testimony of witnesses, the decision regarding the case, and how it was determined by himself; K_259.
One should record this exactly according to the syllables as it was previously stated;
first, one should set down the statements of both the plaintiff and the defendant.
Thereafter, he should cause the decision of the legal treatises (smṛtiśāstra) and the opinion of the court members, the judge, or the families to be recorded right there.
The king, having first shown honor to the plaintiff, should join him with his proven claim and give him a written document bearing his own signature.
And those members of the assembly who are present there, being experts in the treatises on law (smṛti),
should likewise cause their own signatures to be affixed there according to the rules for drawing up documents.
The wise know that a document executed according to this procedure is a *paścātkāra*.
However, where a legal action has been refuted by the plaintiff himself through evidence, a *paścātkāra* may be granted; it is not prescribed in all cases.
To those other than those who are deficient in speech and so forth, [the decision] is granted;
and that which is established by the narration of the facts shall be the document of victory (jayapatra).
[Examination of Documents: Having summoned [the parties] by the king's command, he should investigate according to the law:
a document [is validated] by the conduct regarding documents, and witnesses [by the conduct regarding witnesses]. K_266.

A document that is endowed with proper color, phrasing, and action; that is free from doubt and has clear syllables; and that possesses neither missing order nor missing marks—such a document shall attain validity.
A document is said to be written with the inclusion of local customs, the year, and the increase in months, fortnights, and so forth;
it must bear the hand-signatures of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.
When the letters have fallen from their proper places, are out of order, are indistinct, or deviate from their characteristics,
then that document is considered forged writing.
That which is contrary to local custom, that which is ambiguous, that which lacks proper sequence,
that which is executed by one who is not the owner, and that which is deficient in its object— such [evidence] is defective.
A document executed by one who is intoxicated, by one who fears for his life, by one who is insane, by those who are afflicted,
by women, by children, or by those who are not independent, is not valid.
If, once it has been proclaimed, no one should revoke it on the second day,
then it shall be valid as such, except for that which was performed by one who is intoxicated or insane.
A document may indeed be rendered invalid due to the defect of the witnesses, or that of the scribe,
or through the defect of fraud on the part of either the creditor or the debtor.
A document written by the wicked shall be deemed wicked; one written by the pure, one should declare as pure.
That document [is invalidated] by witnesses, scribes, and executors who are corrupted by fraud.

For those defects of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which are to be stated by the disputant must be made manifest by the members of the assembly at the proper time through the citation of the scriptures, even if they were previously hidden.
Just as the witnesses, the scribe, and the author of the document incur guilt for their falsehood,
so too should faults be attributed to corrupt individuals when a document is corrupted.
"If it was not written by the scribe, nor witnessed by the witnesses," when the defendant has stated this, the document is declared to be forged.
One should not invalidate the means of knowledge through a fault that is not untrue;
for in the case of a false accusation, one shall be punished and shall also lose the object to be proven.
In this way, when a case involving a wicked person is being adjudicated in the king's court,
he should deliberate together with the Brahmins and examine the defects of the written document.
By that [same criterion] by which witnesses, scribes, and officials fall into falsehood, by that the document shall be deemed corrupt; one should declare it valid when the parties are pure.
A document written by the creditor’s own hand, even if devoid of witnesses,
shall be considered forged unless the maker can prove, "It was done by me."
If the debtor denies a signature in his own hand that was placed on the document,
he shall be questioned by the witnesses recorded in the document or according to the opinion of the scribe.

In disputes concerning what has been done or left undone, the decision is reached through witnesses and documentary evidence; if the document is challenged, the plaintiff must point out those who were present when it was recorded.
Confusion may arise for people regarding even the three types of written documents;
therefore, one should establish their validity through the testimony of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.
Now, if the scribe together with the witnesses has met his death, he shall be cleared by means of their own handwriting and so forth; of this there is no doubt.
When there is doubt regarding a debt, whether the debtor is living or dead,
the determination of that document is made by other documents written in his own hand.
Even in the ocean, in the written record, all those who have died remain;
for that which is written is authoritative even when they have passed away.
Direct perception is never sublated by inference;
therefore, the testimony of witnesses may override a defective written document.

For a decision regarding one's own property indeed invalidates the document itself; a written document must be countered by another written document, and that which is supported by witnesses must be countered by witnesses.
In the case of a false statement, one should clear the document by means of the testimony of witnesses and the scribe; he who does not do so shall be made to pay the highest fine for forgery.
If a person who is capable does not request a loan from a wealthy man standing nearby,
that document may be rendered invalid due to the suspicion that it is merely for the sake of clearing a debt.
A document that is more than thirty years old, and which has neither been seen nor heard of,
does not attain validity, even though witnesses may still exist.
But when the profit has been received and the debt is settled, he who does not produce the written document,
nor even asks the debtor for it, shall not obtain its fulfillment.
Thereafter, one should carefully examine whatever is recorded as the cause;
if it is indeed consistent with reason, then that written document shall be considered authoritative.
Otherwise,
the matter should be re-examined from the beginning if something untrue has been established as true due to a lapse in knowledge;
such a judgment must be set aside, even if it was executed with great effort by kings.

A royal edict attains purity when it is purified by the seal, purified by the formal act, purified by the distribution of benefits, provided with its insignia, and authenticated by the king’s own hand.
But that document which is proclaimed to be free from defects shall attain validity.
If the debtor, upon seeing the document, does not point out manifest defects,
then the document shall remain valid for twenty years from that time.
A document by which property is enjoyed for twenty years in the presence of a capable person is free from defects.
If a pledge has been enjoyed for twenty years with absolute certainty,
its validity is established by that document, provided it is free from defects of the writing.
When a dispute over boundaries has been settled, a boundary-deed (sīmāpatra) is to be prepared;
its defects must be declared for a period of twenty years.
Where a debt, together with its principal, is recorded in a document,
they know that it remains valid as evidence even when witnesses have died, provided the amount involved is small.
If something has been received by him, or if a gift has been given without being formally specified,
even without a seal, such a written document is authoritative when witnesses are deceased.
If anything has been received, or if a formal designation has been made,
then the document itself is indeed authoritative, even if the witnesses have died.
A document is established as valid in all cases— provided it was presented at the proper time, accepted, and likewise reminded of— even when the witnesses have died.
A written document is never invalidated even by divine witnesses;
for the law of writing is always superior, and thus it is not set aside by anything else.
The act of writing should always be avoided by means of a counter-document associated with that [original] or one superior to it; it can never be avoided by any other means.
Just as a reflection in a mirror appears to exist though it is non-existent,
so too do skilled people create images for painting.
A document that is handed over to another after having received property, one that is concealed, one that has been tampered with by another, or one kept in the house of someone else; K_309.
Whether the transaction has already taken place or the object exists, provided it was previously recorded in writing,
this very rule is to be understood as the means for determining the validity of the document.
He who forges a document concerning the sale or mortgage of immovable property shall be properly punished by having his tongue, hands, and feet cut off.
If it is marred by stains, burnt, perforated, or even worn out, one should have another painting made; likewise, if it is scratched by sweat, one should do the same.
Written documents, witnesses, and possession are accepted as the three means of proof. Among these proofs, for men, possession is traditionally held to be equal to a written document.
In cases where there is doubt regarding the exit from a street, a gate, a watercourse, and so forth,
it is the settled conclusion that possession alone is the weightiest among the means of proof.
An eyewitness is superior to inference; a written document is superior to eyewitnesses;
and possession by three generations, when unopposed, is more authoritative than these.
Neither the one who seizes them nor their son should exert force for the purpose of using cattle, women, men, and so forth; such is the established law.
Enjoyment is said to be of two kinds: with lineage (sāgamā) and likewise without lineage (anāgamā).
That which extends through three generations and is independent is [enjoyment] with lineage; however, if it is short in duration, it is without lineage.
Possession inherited from a grandfather is considered primary, as is that inherited from a father;
when uninterrupted by these three, such possession lasting sixty years is regarded as firm.
But when that which was eaten by someone with witnesses is proven to have been properly consumed, the claimant shall recover it; it must never be withheld from him.
When a plaintiff has lost a written document or lacks a title deed, but possesses possession,
he must declare the duration of time, the evidence, and the gift in the assembly.
In the period of memory (smārtakāla), possession of land is held to be valid when accompanied by a title;
in the period beyond memory (asmārta), due to the absence of such a record, it is valid through succession over three generations.
In the beginning, however, there is the title-deed; in the middle, possession accompanied by it.
But where possession alone is continuous for three generations, that is the sole title-deed.
The acquirer, even if possessed of possession, shall clear the defects of the document;
his son, however, shall clear the defects of possession, but shall not incur the defects of the document.
For whatever property has been taken up by someone, he alone is entitled to recover it;
even if it has been enjoyed for a long time, possession is not held to belong to anyone other than him.
Out of greed, one should not disturb an enjoyment that has been possessed for a long time and is not clearly defined.

But whatever property was enjoyed by the father according to custom and in accordance with dharma, once he has passed away, it need not be contested; for that which was acquired through enjoyment belongs to him.
But if land has been enjoyed by three persons in succession according to the prescribed rule,
then even in the absence of documentary evidence, a fourth person may acquire it there.
Just as milk produces curd endowed with its own flavor after a period of time,
so too does the cause of a gift result in enjoyment for three generations after a lapse of time.
In the scriptures, possession that is continuous and long-standing is powerful;
even if it has been interrupted, it should be understood as such if it was previously established.
One should not conceive of [the property] as enjoyment in the case of women, the wealth of a king, or the gods;
nor in the case of children, Vedic scholars, or wealth, which proceeds respectively from the mother and the father.
A man seeking wealth might practice celibacy for thirty-six years without observing the vows, or he might dwell for a long time in another country.
Having returned home, one who has not yet taken up the vows should then seek his own wealth;
possession for fifty years constitutes the seizure of that wealth.
It is traditionally taught that twelve years is the period for those seeking knowledge;
for those seeking the knowledge of crafts, it is proclaimed to last until they have mastered them.
Whatever property of theirs was enjoyed by friends and kinsmen while they were unaware,
and that which belonged to those who offended the king, does not perish with the passage of time.

Whatever has been enjoyed by kinsmen of the same lineage, by relatives, and likewise by one's own people—there can be no success through such enjoyment; one should arrange for that enjoyment elsewhere.
[The Principle: But he who, being requested by a petitioner, does not provide assistance—
after three, four, or five times— he becomes a debtor to that other person.
Giving, causing [them] to understand, creating division, the act of enticing,
and indeed the removal of the mind— these are the causes that bring about their destruction.
Whichever among these has been established by the proponent, that shall constitute the fundamental proof; however, when the proponent's claim is refuted, the burden of proof falls upon him.
The king must not allow a delay in the testimony of witnesses;
for through time, a great evil arises characterized by the turning away from Dharma.
The king himself should examine the witnesses who have been presented;
he should examine the statement spoken by the witnesses together with the members of the court.
The time for witnesses to be summoned is when there is a need for a full understanding of the correct course of action;
however, where the testimony is doubtful, one should settle the dispute immediately and clearly.
Within the assembly, the presiding judge, consoling them, shall appoint all the witnesses in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant according to this rule:
Whatever you two know of each other’s mutual conduct regarding this matter, tell it all in truth; for you are the witnesses here.
In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the pure judge should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they face either northward or eastward.
Having summoned the witnesses— who are all of known conduct and who understand the matter— one should question them individually after restraining them with solemn oaths.
But that testimony of witnesses which has been personally experienced due to the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant must be accepted; otherwise, it is not so, according to Bṛhaspati.
Those who are of renowned family and character, free from greed and delusion,
trustworthy, pure, and distinguished— their testimony is undoubtedly valid.
A witness should be examined by the litigant as he is;
one should always have him examined by witnesses who are of equal status, neither superior nor inferior.
Bhṛgu spoke to the wearers of sectarian marks, the guilds and corporations, the merchant associations, and others who exist as collectives, as well as to whatever other groups there may be.
Among the groups of slaves, wandering performers, wrestlers, and those who live by elephants, horses, and weapons—
each of these collectives has its leaders and members;
their disputes within their own groups are settled by those members acting as witnesses.
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men;
virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of low birth for those of the lowest castes.
Where it is impossible for residents of foreign lands to arrive,
one should employ documentary evidence sent by those learned in the three Vedas as testimony.
In the case of a deposit, however, even a single witness may be declared;
even a single messenger sent by the plaintiff becomes a witness.
Whatever commodity has been refined by someone, that person alone shall determine its value;
he alone is declared to be the authority in a dispute concerning it.
The scribe, the presiding judge, and the members of the court, in their respective order,
are declared to be witnesses when they observe the case while the king is looking on.
Furthermore, other witnesses have been declared who are not specifically designated:
the village community, the presiding judge, and the king for those engaged in legal proceedings.
One who is an insider in the affairs [of the family], one who has been sent by the plaintiff,
and those of the same lineage in disputes concerning lineages— these also shall be witnesses.
But when a dispute regarding the division of inheritance arises and doubt is present, the testimony of the kinsmen is the authority in that case; in their absence, [the testimony of] others.
If among the witnesses— whether they be written down or specified by the plaintiff—
one should speak otherwise than the truth, then all of them cease to be witnesses due to that breach of unanimity.
For one person should not cause another who was made a witness by someone else to litigate that case;
in the absence of such a person, however, either an appointed representative or a kinsman may litigate it.
Furthermore, those who derive their livelihood from him, those who perform services for him,
his kinsmen, friends, servants, and trusted associates are not to be witnesses.
Daughters of maternal aunts, sons of uterine brothers, and sons of maternal uncles—these are declared to be "sapindas" (blood relations); one should not employ them as witnesses.
Kinsmen, relatives by marriage, the husband of one's sister, the father, a paternal relative, a paternal uncle, the father-in-law, and likewise teachers; K_363.
Those royal officials who are appointed to positions in cities, villages, and districts, as well as those who are favorites, shall not be questioned; they are devoted to the king.
One should examine witnesses in cases such as debts and in matters of fixed transactions;
however, in cases of violence and urgent offenses, examination is prescribed only in certain instances.
In cases of obstruction of the king’s command, in matters of seizure and acts of violence,
and likewise in cases of theft and verbal assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely.
If the accusation concerns what occurred within a house at night or outside a village,
one should not examine witnesses in these cases.
Testimony should never be spoken by witnesses unless they are questioned by the plaintiff;
no testimony is required from them, for each should apply it to himself.
The written record, the reply, and the witness are endowed with two paths.
Then, standing with his own hand placed upon it, he alone should remain;
if he does not recognize it, one should establish its identity by means of his own hands.
One who is brought by the plaintiff himself and recorded in the document is called a "written witness" (likhita-sākṣin); such a witness exists even without a formal written record [of his testimony].
But that witness who, having seen the matter, is reminded again and again by the plaintiff for the sake of establishing the case, is here called "one who has been reminded."
One who has been brought for a specific purpose and one who has arrived by chance—
these two witnesses, even if not recorded in writing, are effective in proving the plaintiff's case.
One who, remaining hidden, has been clearly informed by a plaintiff for the sake of establishing his own case regarding the statement of the defendant,
is called a hidden witness.
That witness who gives testimony again and again,
whether by hearing it himself or by causing others to hear it, is designated as an *uttara-sākṣin* (a witness for the reply).
He whose secrets are disclosed through trust, or who is informed of a mission, should be known as a secret agent; likewise, one who has mastered the task [is also such].
Where the plaintiff has perished, there the witness is one whose testimony is based on what was heard at the time of death;
and where the defendant has perished, it is likewise prescribed in that case.

[The disclosure of defects in witnesses: Whatever defects of the document may exist, as well as those attributed to the witnesses, must be stated at the time of the trial; one should not raise them after they have already been spoken.
But he who, regarding the meaning of what has been stated, should maliciously attack witnesses who have not been previously discredited,
and does not state the grounds for that [attack], shall incur the first amercement.
One should not invalidate a means of valid cognition through a fault that is not untrue;
however, for making a false accusation, one shall be punished and shall also lose the matter to be proven.
Furthermore, when the defendant or the plaintiff establishes a defect in the witnesses,
it does not constitute a separate legal proceeding, because it is relevant to the matter at hand.
The defects of the witnesses must be stated by the defendant in the assembly;
having written all of them down on a document, he should then state his reply.
But they can never serve as witnesses regarding the actual practice [of the rite];
therefore, they must be meditated upon otherwise by the defendant through ritual action.

If the defendant fails to substantiate his claim, he shall be compelled to pay the debt; likewise, all witnesses who have been produced must clearly prove their case, for those who fail to do so are excluded from the status of witnesses by the law of testimony.
One should discern the internal state of that person through their facial expressions, gestures, and movements;
the opponent will be seen as defeated by means of this inference.
Trembling, perspiration, agitation, and the touching of the lips when they are dry; scratching the ground, loss of one's position, looking sideways or upwards,
and a change in the voice— these the wise declare to be the signs of a corrupted [witness].
Witnesses must give their testimony while remaining within the assembly hall, and not elsewhere;
for this rule applies to all types of testimony, except in cases concerning immovable property.
In the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant, and in the presence of the matter to be proven, the witness must testify directly; under no circumstances should he do so in their absence.
The matter should be stated above those two as well, even in their absence;
this rule applies to four-footed creatures and to bipeds and immovable beings.
One may dispute even in the absence of balances, weights, or measures;
however, in all formal transactions, one cannot act as a witness otherwise than in accordance with those means.
If there is a killing of living beings, one should cause the testimony to be proclaimed in the presence of Śiva;
in the absence of that, however, one should proclaim it by means of a sign, and not otherwise.
The testimony of those witnesses, when stated spontaneously and free from defects, is to be accepted;
once the witnesses have spoken, they should not be questioned again by the king.
Whatever they might say by way of its very nature is to be accepted as conventional;
therefore, whatever else they might speak regarding the Dharma is meaningless.
But that which is seen by those assembled together must be stated exactly as it was;
however, that which concerns individual tasks performed separately must be stated individually.
But when a matter is learned by witnesses at different times, one should have them state it individually; for Bhṛgu has declared that such is a case occurring at different times.
In disputes concerning debts and the like, which are generally of a stable nature, once a decision has been reached,
the matter to be proved is not established even if the stated amount is deficient or excessive.
Even when the portion of the matter to be proven has been stated by the witnesses, the entire case shall be established;
this applies to matters involving sexual intercourse, violence, and theft, as well as whatever else has been determined to be the point at issue.
But where there may be a deficiency or an excess, one should reject that testimony;
in such a case, the witness should not be punished, for he deserves punishment for failing to speak.
Where a witness contradicts [the facts regarding] the place, time, wealth, number, form, caste, appearance, or age, the wise know that testimony to be unspoken.
When the various matters have been set forth and the witness has arrived for testimony, if he does not speak in accordance with the facts, that testimony is not considered properly delivered.
Where witnesses state a matter either less than or more than it actually is, that too should be known as improper; this is the determination regarding witnesses.
[The Faults and Punishments of Witnesses:
"If they speak entirely without being questioned, or likewise fail to speak when questioned,
witnesses shall be restrained, censured, and punished according to the law."
In cases of verbal abuse, fraud, or dispute, they shall be fined three hundred panas;
in disputes concerning debts and the like, they shall likewise be made to pay the money and the debt itself.
That lowest of men who, though not designated as a witness, nor summoned, nor even presented,
should speak either falsely or even the truth, he too is to be punished.
If a witness does not state the testimony, he shall pay the debt and carry an equal fine;
for other disputes, he deserves a fine of three hundred.
And those who, having spoken one way, speak otherwise, being possessed of verbal quibbling, should be punished.
Having seized all the property of one by whose greed for gain false witnesses were appointed, the king should thereafter banish him from the realm.
When the matter to be proven has been established by witnesses for the plaintiff,
if the defendant should prove that case otherwise,
or if there be many witnesses of noble birth, the former witnesses shall be considered false witnesses.
When an action is purified through the proper method, then there is the purification of its verbal expression;
and that which is purified from a purified verbal expression is the purified meaning—this is the established principle.
One should recognize that a witness speaks falsely when, within seven days,
or within fourteen or twenty-one days, or even within forty-six days depending on the nature of the object and other factors, there occurs disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman.
[And their divine ordeals pertaining to the subject matter of the points of dispute:
No one should cause the accuser to undergo the divine ordeals; those expert in divine ordeals should administer the ordeal to the accused. K_411.
For those who are suspected by kings, one should employ the balance and other such ordeals;
however, in the performance of self-purification, one should not include the head ordeal therein.

For those who are defiled by public scandal and those suspected by bandits, scales and other such ordeals should be employed; however, Bhṛgu says that the head-weighing ordeal must never be used in such cases.
One should never employ a head-case in doubtful matters;
rather, one should cause headless divine ordeals to be administered to the king's servants.

In matters of suspicion or establishing trust, in the partitioning of inheritance among heirs, and in the performance of collective undertakings, one should always cause the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) to be administered.
Where there is a denial of what has been given, one should determine the proof;
in cases of theft or violence, one should cause an ordeal to be administered even when the matter is of small value.
Having ascertained the measure of all the substances, one should fashion the gold;
then, endowed with the proper measure of gold, one should employ that divine [image].
Having ascertained the number of gold pieces, it is taught that for a loss of one hundred, one should take poison;
and for a loss of eighty, one should indeed offer oneself into the fire.
If sixty [coins] are lost, water should be administered; for forty, indeed, a jar [of water];
and for the loss of twenty or ten, the drinking of the sacred vessel (kośapāna) is prescribed.
Or, upon the loss of more than five [measures], there should be rice for half of that;
but upon the loss of half of that again, one should touch the head of a son or another relative.
But when even half of that half has perished, worldly activities are prescribed;
reflecting thus, a king does not fall away from dharma and artha.

[The regulations concerning divine ordeals according to the caste and craft of the plaintiff and defendant: One should employ fire for a Kṣatriya, the water-jar for a Brāhmaṇa, and water for a Vaiśya;
or one may employ any divine ordeal for all castes, except poison, which is to be avoided for the twice-born.
He should cause those twice-born men who are cattle-herders, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers to be treated like Śūdras.

One should never administer fire to metalworkers, water to those who subsist on water, nor poison to those who know the application of mantras. One should not employ rice-grains as an ordeal for one observing a vow or for one suffering from diseases of the mouth.
One should avoid fire for those suffering from skin diseases, water for those with asthma and cough,
and one must always strictly avoid poison for those with disorders of bile and phlegm.
The treasury should not be given by the wise to those addicted to liquor and women, nor to gamblers, nor likewise to those who follow the ways of nihilists.
[This applies] to those who kill their mother, father, a twice-born, a guru, children, women, or a king;
to those burdened with the great sins (mahāpātaka); and especially to atheists (nāstika).
But for those who bear the marks [of asceticism], who are deceitful, who know the rituals of mantra and yoga,
who are born of mixed castes, and who persist in the practice of evil—
In these very charges and in those that are blameworthy, a king devoted to righteousness should not, with any effort, administer an ordeal.
For virtuous persons appointed by these very [means], the ordeal is divine;
but where the virtuous do not accept it, those to be cleared must be tested by their own men.
The ordeal must not be administered to those guilty of mortal sins, especially to atheists,
nor to those who are habitually devoted to sinful acts.
In these legal proceedings, divine ordeals are strictly prohibited;
however, one should have them performed by virtuous persons, for Manu says that one who has been falsely accused should not be abandoned.
In the case of those who are untouchable, low-caste slaves, barbarians (mlecchas), evildoers,
or born of inverse unions (prātilomya), there is no fixed rule regarding the king;
one should prescribe for them in cases of doubt those ordeals that are well-known among them.

[The divine regions: One should employ these in the presence of the king for those men who have been accused in the abode of Indra, who are great sinners, and who have engaged in treason against the sovereign.
For those born of inverse unions (prātilomya), the ordeal should be administered at a crossroads;
for others, the wise know that the ordeal should be administered in the midst of the assembly hall.
