But when there is a conflict between time and place, one should determine what is appropriate;
in such a case of reversal, one should have another person undergo the ordeal—this is the rule.
Those [mantras] given at an improper place or time, or those performed outside of the dwelling,
undoubtedly cause deviation from the true goals in this world.
If there is a contradiction in the proof, one must establish that which is to be proven once again;
for even if the divine ordeals have been administered as prescribed,
the king should avoid them when they are performed by fools, the greedy, or the wicked, and indeed, those ordeals must be administered anew.
Therefore, the experts should administer the ordeal according to the prescribed rule;
for when applied contrary to the rule, it is not capable of establishing the truth.
If the sling breaks, the balance beam snaps, or likewise the cord,
or if there is doubt regarding purity, one should examine the man again.

[The Procedure for the Fire Ordeal]: If the accused stumbles or is burned at a place other than the designated spot, the gods do not consider him burnt; one should have him undergo the ordeal once more.
[The Procedure for the Water Ordeal] For the sake of purity, one should prepare arrows with tips not made of iron;
they may even be made of bamboo, and the thrower should discharge them with great firmness.
When [the opponent] has been cast [into the water], he must perform the immersion; the departure [of the challenger] and the arrival [of the defendant] must be simultaneous.
Upon the departure, however, the arrival must be made; another man shall enter the water.
If, upon entering the water, only the crown of the head is seen while neither the ears nor the nose are visible, one should declare that person to be pure.
If a man who has submerged himself is seen by living beings as he emerges,
he should submerge again at that very spot, once it has been identified by local landmarks.
[The Procedure for the Poison and Divine Ordeals:
That which resembles a goat's horn, dark green, very thick, and originating from a horn;
and which, when broken, has the appearance of ginger—that is known as the poison of horned animals.
One should make that red and black, and likewise hard according to its characteristics;
by this method, it should be known as divine by those skilled in the divine.
Yellow, resembling the *vatsanābha* [poison], this is the certainty through the knowledge of its color;
one should recognize that which has the shape of a pearl or a conch shell when broken as being *vatsanābhaka*.
When combined with honey and milk, it becomes clear in that very instant;
thus has the external characteristic been explained by those who accomplish the Dharma.
In the forenoon, one should administer poison to living beings in a cool place,
having ground it finely and mixed with thirty times its weight of clarified butter.
From six palas of poison, that portion which is the twentieth part should be taken;
from that, reduced by one-eighth, it should be given to the person to be cleared, immersed in clarified butter.
[The Procedure for the Divine Treasure] When there is a minor offense, one should bathe the gods with water from their weapons;
if the person undergoes a physical change, they are impure and must be restrained, otherwise they are pure.
[The Procedure for Rice:
When the water used for the bathing and drinking of the deity is consumed as divine rice, one becomes pure by spitting it out cleanly; otherwise, one is impure and must be restrained.
Even if a person is pure in terms of his treasury, if he is accused by one who is backed by force,
the righteous king should compel the accuser to pay both a fine and the legal costs; however,
if the man is proven pure by ordeal, the king should honor him.
Where blood is seen, and the jaw-hair droops,
and whose body trembles— one should designate him as impure.

Then, if there is a discrepancy with the divine ordeal, after three times seven days, one should compel the accused to pay that amount as well as a fine, having exerted effort [to prove his innocence].
If that [calamity] should befall only one person and not all people,
then he is liable for the disease, fire, death of a kinsman, the debt, and must pay a fine.
Consumption, diarrhea, eruptive boils, pain in the palate and bones,
eye disease, throat disease,
as well as insanity, headache, and the breaking of the arms— these are the divine afflictions that arise for men.
One who is pure should be made to pay fifty; one who is impure shall be subject to punishment.
One should prescribe punishment in accordance with the sequence of poison, water, fire, the balance, the sacred vessel, rice grains, and the ordeal of the heated gold coin.
One should arrange one thousand, six hundred, five hundred,
and likewise four, three, two, or even one [of the deities] in descending order for those who are inferior.
[The Procedure for Oaths:
Where a ritual action is prescribed but it is not stated which limb of the performer is to be used,
the right hand should be understood as the one that brings the rites to completion.
He for whom no terrible calamity, whether caused by the king or by fate, occurs until the fourteenth day [from the oath], is to be known as pure in his oath.

[An investigation into acts performed by those who are insane or lacking autonomy: Whatever is given or whatever is done by one who is insane, intoxicated, or likewise in another state of mind— that shall not be considered valid.
The master shall annul any transaction performed by one who is not independent;
no one other than the master may contest it, except for that which was done by one who is terrified, insane, or otherwise lacking independence.
A father who lacks independence, a son who has a father, a brother, or even a nephew;
likewise a younger brother whose property is undivided, a slave, or a laborer.
The gifting, mortgaging, or selling of fields, houses,
or slaves does not achieve validity if performed by one who is not independent, nor if they have not been duly described.
All of these are authoritative in the buying and selling of merchandise,
provided that they are approved even as they carry out their transactions.
In the same way, brothers, nephews, or sons may act as representatives for fields and other matters,
provided they have been authorized by their elder to perform the necessary duties when he departs.
But he who has been authorized with full power regarding a particular matter is indeed the master in that matter;
his employer cannot undo the business transacted by him otherwise.
A father has authority over his son and his wife in matters of instruction;
however, he has no authority over his son regarding sale or gift.
[The function of determination: Purification has been declared by those who know the true principles of the scriptures to be medical treatment;
it is recorded as being of two kinds: expiation and punishment.
Even when multiple claims are brought forward, the creditor receives only as much wealth as he can prove with witnesses;
for that much alone is the wealth considered proven.
Bṛhaspati states that if a person, having made a total denial, should later admit even a small portion of it privately, he must be made to pay the entire amount when formally accused.
Thus, seated upon the Dharma-throne, the judge, being impartial, should observe the determination of legal cases together with Brahmins, and not otherwise.
Having personally examined the legal proceedings, or having heard them from the presiding judge,
the king should then issue a certificate of victory for the sake of official recognition.
[The Procedure for Punishment:
But the king should cause a Brahmin to pay the debt to the owner by means of conciliation alone;
however, he should cause others who are wicked to pay by afflicting them according to the customs of the region.
Bhṛgu declared that one should cause even an heir or a friend to pay by means of deception; this applies to merchants, farmers, and artisans as well.
Having ascertained that he is unable to pay the fine, one should compel him to perform labor under one's own supervision;
if he is incapable of even that, he should be cast into prison, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa.
But one should cause the cultivators—whether they be Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—who are making an effort, to pay [the tax].
In the case of offenses against the teacher, the father, the mother, and likewise one's kinsmen,
no punishment whatsoever is ordained for them.
But where an improper act has been committed during a life-threatening emergency, there shall be no punishment at all; this is the law remembered by Bhṛgu.
One must never kill a Brahmin, even if he is established in every kind of sin;
rather, one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and unhurt.
For members of all four castes who fail to perform expiation,
the king shall prescribe a lawful punishment involving both their person and their wealth.
Whatever punishment is prescribed by law for a Śūdra for a particular offense,
that same punishment shall be doubled for both a Kṣatriya and a Brāhmaṇa.
A Śūdra who has entered the life of a renunciant and is devoted to the recitation of prayers and burnt offerings,
if he commits a sin, should be punished with death or fined double the usual penalty.
In all offenses, whatever monetary fine is prescribed for a man, women shall pay half of that; however, in the case of killing, the man's limb shall be cut off.
Women who are not independent should not be held accountable; it is the man therein who commits the offense.
They are to be disciplined by their master, but the king shall bring the man to justice.
If a woman whose husband is away from home is apprehended,
she shall be kept in confinement until her lord has returned.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed for a particular offense must be diligently applied; it shall consist of the collection of fines in paṇas, or else its equivalent value paid to the king.
Wherever a fine is imposed, whether it be a quarter-māṣa or two māṣas, it should be understood as unspecified; however, one should calculate it as being one māṣaka.
Where a fine is stated in *māṣakas*, one should specify it as being in silver;
where it is stated in *kṛṣṇalas*, that indeed shall be the determination of the stated fine.
A māṣa should be known as one-twentieth of a kārṣāpaṇa;
a kākaṇī, however, is one-fourth of a māṣaka and of a paṇa.
In the region of the Five Rivers, this is the conventional terminology:
four *kārṣāpaṇa*-coins are known as one *dhānaka*;
twelve of those are a *suvarṇa*; and a *dīnāra* is recorded as being equal to a *citraka*.
[Furthermore, the principle:

That position which is determined by the members of the court as "it is non-existent" or "it is existent" is declared to be "decided," whereas that which is "instructed" is proclaimed to be based on the testimony of witnesses.
But if someone does not attain satisfaction even when [the truth] has been ascertained by the family and others,
the king, having investigated that matter, should set aside what was done wrong and restore it.
[Consideration of Interest in the Non-payment of Debt:
One should never grant a loan to women, slaves, or children;
the lender shall not recover that [interest], but he may give them whatever wealth [he wishes].
However, whatever interest exceeding [the legal rate] has been stipulated by the debtor,
being contracted during a time of distress, must always be paid;
but that which was stipulated otherwise need not be paid under any circumstances.
But where one should clear off the interest only when the principal has increased by a fixed amount,
and the debtor pays it at the appointed time, that is known as *śikhāvṛddhi*.
Satisfaction is proclaimed as the fruit from the house, and the acquisition of enjoyments from the field.
But that which is entirely for the purpose of enjoyment, where interest is merely nominal,
and where the application [of the loan] is likewise, is called *ādhibhoga*.
[Ākṛtavṛddhi]:
If one who has taken a loan should depart for another region without having returned it,
that debt shall accrue interest for him after the lapse of one year.
If one who has been requested for a loan takes it and departs for another region without making a repayment or providing interest,
that debt shall begin to accrue interest after three months have passed.
But if one who resides even in his own country does not pay when requested at any time,
the creditor shall compel him to pay interest that has not yet been incurred, even if he is unwilling.
A gift given out of affection does not increase so long as it has not been asked for;
if it is not returned when requested, it increases by five percent per month.
Interest on a deposit, the remainder of interest, and likewise profit from buying and selling—
if these are not paid when requested, they increase by five percent per hundred.
If one who has taken merchandise should depart for another region without paying the price,
that person shall be liable for interest on that wealth after three seasons have passed.
Interest shall never accrue on leather, grain, liquor, stakes in gambling, the price of goods, the bride-price for women, nor on amounts received as surety.
The amount of interest to be taken shall always be double the principal lent by creditors;
if it does not reach double, one may calculate further interest.
The price of gems, pearls, corals, gold, silver, and of wrought iron,
raw silk, and wool increases twofold.
The increase for all types of oils, as well as for liquors, clarified butter,
molasses, and salt, should be known to be eightfold.
Base metals are considered to be fivefold [the value of the land], and land is likewise considered eightfold;
because of the statement "immediately," it is paid immediately.
[The Settlement of Debt] [The Rule for When Multiple Debts Are Combined]:
One should discharge a debt that was recorded on the same day in its entirety.
Grasping, guarding, and gaining [are the functions], whereas otherwise they follow in their respective order.
But when there is a combination of various debts, whatever was contracted first must be paid first;
after that, the king's debt shall be paid, followed by that of the Vedic scholar (śrotriya).
If one should prove that a commodity was acquired by means of another's property, that property must be returned by the debtor himself; it cannot be otherwise.
If, having taken an object as collateral, one gives it for the purpose of interest so that it may be used,
whether it be movable or immovable, that is called a pledge for use (bhogyādhi).
Having paid a higher price than that, one may acquire one's own field and so forth.
If one should make a claim against two [parties], what procedure should be followed?
Of those two, the prior claim should be accepted; the one who made it later shall receive the punishment of a thief.
When a document concerning a mortgage, sale,
or gift is found to contradict a single legal act through the testimony of witnesses, that document is considered fraudulent.
Kātyāyana declared that what is not specified, what is specified, and what is written down in one place are all superseded by that which is specifically written down as a particular rule.
If one were to first assume something non-existent, whose nature is unindicated and which is like space, that [assumption] would itself remain unindicated;
whatever might exist for him at that time, he should point out as being indicated.
But when one has first designated all one's property and subsequently deposits it marked with one's name,
how could that not be more powerful as a means of identification?
When a field or even a village is marked by boundary signs,
and the villages and so forth are recorded [in writing], then one shall attain success.
But whatever has been pledged as collateral that is destroyed through the act of fate or the king,
the debtor must pay the debt to the creditors along with interest.
If, however, [the pledge] should perish or the debtor should die through no fault of the creditor,
the debtor shall be released from the debt, and the creditor shall be made to provide another pledge.
If one should compel a person to perform work against their will and without their consent, he shall be made to pay the fruit of that labor; he does not receive interest.
But he who, while another is performing work as a pledge, should harass or threaten him with words, with a staff, or by his actions,
shall incur the first amercement.
If one should forcibly enter a pledge that was not surrendered against one's will,
he shall incur the first degree of violence, and the depositor shall recover his pledge.
If a creditor enjoys a pledge through a fraudulent document from a debtor,
the king, having caused him to pay a fine, shall cause that fraudulent pledge-deed to be destroyed.

But where there is no depositor, the creditor shall report the pledge to the king; it is the settled rule that he may then sell it publicly. Having received the amount together with interest, he should hand over the remainder to the king.
[The Procedure for a Surety]:

In matters of gifts, attendance, and disputes, as well as for the purpose of trust and oaths, one should certainly cause a surety (*lagnaka*) to be taken; in other cases, it should be done accordingly.
If a surety for appearance does not produce the defendant at the proper place and time,
he shall pay the debt there, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
For the purpose of searching for what has been lost, however, a period of up to three fortnights should be granted;
if he can produce it there, the surety shall be released.
If, when the time has passed, the guarantor does not produce that person, he shall be compelled to pay that debt; the same rule is ordained even in the case of his death.
Wherever a mortgage has been taken such that the creditor remains secured by it,
the son shall be made to pay that debt from that property, even in the absence of the father.
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance,
he shall pay the debt from his own property to that person if he fails to produce him.
The first two [types of witnesses] shall be made to pay the wealth that was not disclosed at the time [of the transaction], provided it is false;
however, in the case of a contradiction, the latter two shall be made to pay, as shall their sons in their absence.
If the father is away on a journey, the son should pay all debts incurred while they were under one roof;
however, Bṛhaspati maintains that when the father has died, the son need not pay the father's share of a debt contracted with others.
When those who have entered under a single liability are seen there, he should be made to pay;
if the debtor has gone abroad, his son must pay the whole; but if the father is dead, the son must pay his paternal share.
But he who, being oppressed, gives a surety while under pressure,
is entitled to receive double the amount of that debt after three fortnights have passed.
That for whose sake, by whom, and on what grounds a surety was given according to the prescribed rule and with the consent of the witnesses, that surety shall receive that very thing.
In the event of a breach of a solemn agreement, one should cause double the amount to be paid;
for if he does not do so, that [agreement] shall be lost—this is the purpose of a solemn agreement.

One should know that a debt contracted by a father or others for the sake of the family, when taken by one who is incapable or afflicted by illness, or for the purpose of averting a calamity, is indeed a debt incurred in times of distress.
Whatever has been done for the marriage of a daughter or for funeral rites—
all this must be given to the master by the family, O Lord.
According to the law, a debt incurred by a son need not be paid by the father;
however, that which was promised or that which was subsequently approved must be paid.
Bhṛgu says that even if the absent husband has not given his consent, a debt contracted for the sake of the family must be paid by the wife,
a female slave, the mother, a pupil, or a son.
A debt contracted in this manner—whether jointly with a husband or a son, or by oneself alone—must be paid; otherwise, that which was contracted by a woman [alone] need not be paid.

If a woman is declared by her husband who intends to die, "This debt must be paid by you," she shall be compelled to pay it even if she has not agreed to it, provided that wealth was entrusted to her.
Even if he is afflicted by disease or has gone abroad from his own country,
a debt incurred by a father must be paid by his sons after twenty years have passed.
In such cases, one should compel even the sons to pay the debt of those who are diseased, insane, aged, or long absent from home, even while they are still living.
Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons if it has been proven;
however, this does not apply to those who are blind from birth, outcasts, insane, or afflicted with consumption, leprosy, and similar diseases.
Since fathers are liberated from their lowest debt only by means of the gifts given by the sons who have been born to them,
for that reason fathers desire sons.
When the father has died, the inheritance should never be given by one who has not yet attained legal capacity;
however, it must be bestowed at the proper time according to the prescribed rule, otherwise they shall dwell in hell.
If one who has not attained legal majority is independent even here, he is liable for debt;
for independence is traditionally held to reside in the eldest, being produced by seniority, virtue, and age.
That which was seen [by the father], or what remains of a gift, or that which was inherited from a grandfather—such a debt may be paid.
However, a debt that is defective or was opposed by the father must never be paid under any circumstances.
Bhṛgu says that a debt seen by the father, which has descended in succession from the grandfather,
must be paid by the grandsons even if it was not discharged by the sons, provided it is free from defect.
But that ancestral property which was not given by the sons while they were living in a state of illness—
of such a kind, the paternal grandfather’s share must be given equally by the grandsons.
One should compel the son to pay the debt if he is free from misfortune, capable of wealth, and fit for the burden; otherwise, one should not compel the son to pay.
Whatever must always be given by the fathers, that should be paid from their estate in their absence;
or else that debt must be paid by the sons or the grandsons to the owner of that wealth at that time.
If a debt to the ancestors remains unpaid, the son shall not take the inheritance;
that wealth must be given to the creditor, for if he takes it after [the father] has died, he shall be made to pay it back.
In the absence of a son, however, the debt must be paid diligently by the grandson;
it should not be paid by the fourth descendant, for from that point it ceases.
A grandson must never pay a debt incurred through a guarantee;
however, a father’s debt must always be paid by his son, even if he is not yet of age.
The debt must be paid by the inheritor of the estate; in his absence, by the wife;
in her absence, by the sons; and in their absence, by others entitled to inherit the property, in due order.
As long as a son does not obtain his paternal property that is available,
the debtor shall not be made to pay, even if the son is very wealthy.
Whether it be a written document or a verbal promise,
whatever has been promised to a woman who previously belonged to another, one should know that among men such an act is performed out of lust.
For when, having instigated violence or having destroyed property out of anger,
one says something intended to cause satisfaction, one should know that it is an act committed out of anger.
Whether healthy or afflicted, one who has made a formal commitment for the sake of Dharma must give;
if he dies without having given, his son shall be compelled to pay—of this there is no doubt.
But whatever debt has been incurred by those who are destitute, childless, or such as vintners and the like,
the one who enjoys their wives must indeed pay that very debt.
The one who acts as a supervisor for the wives of a vintner, a hunter, a commoner, a cowherd,
or a sailor shall be made to pay their debts incurred in the business of those husbands.

And a debt incurred by a wife shall not in any way become the husband's obligation, except for what was contracted during times of distress; for men have extensive responsibilities for the sake of the family.
Except for the wives of washermen, hunters, cowherds, and liquor-sellers;
for their livelihood is dependent on those [occupations], and their families rely upon them.
If a woman, being without a husband, should resort to another man for the sake of her son,
that wealth must be taken away by the son alone, excluding the daughters.
One should take up the thread for the sake of the debt, never for the sake of pleasure;
for when there is no valid reason, one should not compel the parents to pay.
If a woman who has sons, having taken her own property, should abandon even a capable son,
then, according to Manu, the father’s debt shall be cleared from that [property].
And she who, for the sake of her young son, has resorted to another man—her husband shall pay that debt; this is declared to be the rule regarding one with a young son.
Property belonging to those who have been long absent, to those without kin, to the dull-witted, the insane, the afflicted, or those wearing the marks of a religious order,
must be given away by those who depend upon the property of their wives, even while these individuals are still alive.
When a son is overwhelmed by calamity, or when a minor is seen [in charge], the one who takes the property must pay;
in his absence, the one who takes the wife must pay.
First, the one who takes the wealth shall give;
after him, the one who took the wife; in the absence of a daughter, or the son who is utterly destitute.

A debt contracted by a wife must be paid by the husband, and one contracted by a mother by the son; likewise, that which was contracted for the sake of the husband must be paid if he has gone abroad after having made a declaration.
That which is done for the sake of a son shall be considered as given;
likewise that which has been described, that which was done without being requested, and that which was done after hearing it but not being urged.
But the debtor who has been detained shall be held publicly in an assembly of people until he pays what is due,
according to the established customs of the region.
If a person being carried should feel the urge to void excrement or urine,
he should be followed behind, or one should release him once he has been securely bound.
Having provided a guarantor, he should be released day by day;
at the time of eating and at night, the guarantor remains as a bond.
He who cannot find a surety for his appearance and does not provide one should be confined in prison or kept under guard after being informed of the situation.
A noble person who is trustworthy and pure should not be confined in prison;
whether he is unbound or bound by oath, he should be released.
A creditor who has first attempted persuasion, conciliation, and legal proceedings should recover his debt from the debtor by means of pressure and confinement.
In this manner, he may take wealth through pretext and by means of his conduct;
likewise, he should cause the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—whether they be equal or inferior—to pay tribute through their labor.
One should cause a king, a master, or a Brahmin to pay by means of conciliation alone; however, one may settle the matter with a kinsman or a friend even through a pretext.
Bhṛgu said to merchants, farmers, and artisans:
"They should be made to pay according to the customs of the region; having oppressed those who are wicked, one should cause them to pay."
But where a creditor oppresses a debtor who speaks the truth,
he shall be deprived of that wealth and shall incur a fine equal to it.
For if he should cause [the debtor] to perform an unrighteous act that was not previously commanded at the outset,
the creditor would first incur a fine for violence and be released from his debt.
He who takes a loan or other property and does not return it to the owner is born as a slave,
a servant, a woman, or a beast in that person's house.
A deposit left with a person who has gone abroad,
a pledge, a bailment, a loan for use,
and that which is entrusted as a means of livelihood for a Vaiśya— this is known in law as *upanidhi*.
Whatever has been deposited with someone, that person should protect it with diligence;
any destruction of it other than what is caused by fate or the king is declared to be his own fault.
If anything is destroyed or stolen through his fault,
he shall be made to pay for that property with interest, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
If the object is destroyed immediately after being requested—even if the destruction was caused by fate or the king—the borrower must be made to pay its value; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever property of another— whether deposited with him, consumed by him, neglected by him,
or destroyed through his ignorance— he alone shall be made to restore it.
If [the deposit] is consumed, he shall be made to pay it with interest; if it is neglected, he shall be made to pay the equivalent amount;
if it is destroyed through negligence, he shall be made to pay a small fraction less.
If a deposit, even when not lost through the fault of the king or fate, is destroyed where it was kept,
that loss is said to belong to the depositor along with the goods, provided they were not taken back by the recipient.
But if the giver, having learned of the loss of the goods, deposits them elsewhere,
then even if all other means of recovery fail, the recipient shall not be made to pay.
For whatever has been lost through the fault of the purchaser belongs to the purchaser;
when that [item] is lost or even stolen, the buyer shall pay its value.
The deposit should be accepted at the proper time, but one should avoid accepting it when the time has passed;
for one who returns it after the time has lapsed, a fine is imposed and he is made to pay double the amount.
These rules have been proclaimed for all types of deposits.
If the deposit is processed by the artisan over a fixed number of days, then beyond that period he shall set it aside; even if it is damaged by fate, the artisan must pay for it.
If destruction occurs due to a fault in the installation, that [liability] shall not be imposed upon the artisan;
however, if it is due to a fault in the craftsmanship, he should cause that which was entrusted for the purpose of restoration to be returned.
If even a very small amount of work performed by a servant is lost,
it shall be sufficient cause for that master’s loss, even if he intends to give [the wage] but fails to take hold of it.

If one has been requested for something with a specific purpose in mind or for a fixed time, and that object is not delivered because the purpose was only half-fulfilled or the time had not yet arrived, then he is not made to pay it.
If a task has been performed when the time for it had arrived, one should not pay even when requested;
or, if that [work] has perished, the receiver shall recover the value.
If he does not give when being asked, he shall be compelled to pay it along with interest.
Now, if there is a failure of the work, that loss shall belong to the employer himself;
however, if the time has not yet arrived, he must be made to pay for even half-finished work.
He who, having taken a borrowed item, does not return it when asked, shall be seized by force and compelled to give it back; he who does not give it shall be fined.
When, after the completion of a transaction, one says "You should give this to another at my word," that which is thus delivered is called *anvādhi* (a subsequent pledge) in this context.
[On Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner:
He shall annul a sale by one who is not the owner, as well as a gift or a pledge.
The plaintiff shall first provide the wealth from his own kinsmen;
afterwards, for the sake of his own purification, the purchaser shall provide it through his own relatives.
But the owner of the lost property shall recover his own wealth by making it known through his relatives;
having established that it was not given, abandoned, or sold, he recovers his money.
He should either make a public purchase or present the original source;
however, a period for bringing the source must be granted according to the number of *yojanas*.
One should perform the purchase openly with virtuous kinsmen and one's own people;
no other procedure is prescribed there, whether divine or human.
When, having presented the original source, the proponent further speaks of a purchase, he should simply produce that original source;
there is no need for the purchase.
But one who cannot produce the root source of his possession must clear up the purchase itself;
once the purchase has been cleared up by the king, he should not be questioned about anything further.
If he does not produce the original document or purify the purchase by providing proof of acquisition,
he shall be made to pay the debt to the creditor according to the claim, as well as a fine.
If one who has lost his wealth does not recover it himself, nor through his kinsmen,
he deserves punishment like a thief in order to prevent the recurrence of such incidents.
The owner, having paid half the value, shall take back his own property;
in that case, according to legal procedure, half of both [the price and the stolen object] shall be considered lost.
Failure to recognize the price and likewise failure to protect it—
these two have been declared by the Buddhas to be causes of the loss of wealth.
[Joint Undertaking: Whatever physicians or merchants may be assembled together,
the fruit obtained therein by those who have not divided it among themselves is equal.

Established by a formal agreement (*samaya*), they shall without deviation attend to the inspection of merchandise, the collection of goods, the accounting of expenditures, the removal of waste, and the assessment of the weight and value of the cargo.
But for those who carry out the transaction with gold, grain, liquids, and so forth,
their profit shall be of a corresponding kind, according to whether their shares are equal, deficient, or excessive.
If a single man, being approved by many,
should give wealth or even cause a debt to be incurred, it shall be considered as having been done by all of them.
A debt to kinsmen, relatives, and friends may be paid even with collateral;
for others, it must likewise be accompanied by a guarantor, as well as a written document and witnesses.
Gold may be given at one's own will, as well as liquids and grain according to the prescribed rule;
it should be given and likewise received in accordance with local custom.
But that which is given by those acting in concert must likewise be requested;
whoever does not ask for it is deprived of his gain.
But whoever recovers property from a thief, from water, or from fire, a tenth part of it shall be given to him; this is the rule in all such cases.
Those skilled in training, those possessing supernormal powers, and the preceptor— these artisans shall receive one, two, three, or four shares respectively, in ascending order.
Whatever wealth may have been seized from a foreign kingdom by thieves under the king's command,
they shall divide it according to the rule, having first set aside one-tenth for the king.
The leader of the thieves shall take four shares from that [booty];
the brave one, three shares; the capable one, two; and each of the others who were merely emaciated, one share each.
If any among them who have gone forth should incur a seizure,
they shall bear, according to their respective shares, whatever has been given for the sake of his release.
This indeed is the law declared by the virtuous for dancers:
one who knows the rhythm (tāla) receives half, while the singers receive equal shares;
those who are the leaders deserve two shares—this is the rule for those performing in concert.
This is the decision for all— merchants, farmers, thieves, artisans, and those who set their shares without restraint.
In matters concerning the non-payment of what has been given or the refusal to give what has been promised,
as well as in sales and gifts, those who are unwilling should not be coerced;
however, one may personally employ one's own wife, sons, and all property.
In times of distress, however, giving away or even selling [the property] may be performed;
otherwise it should not be undertaken—such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
Except for his entire estate and his home, whatever property exceeds what is necessary for the maintenance of his family may be given away; otherwise, it shall not be given.
Therefore, while a father has authority over his children and wife in matters of instruction,
he does not have such authority over his son regarding sale or gift.
He who, having voluntarily promised a gift to a Brāhmaṇa,
does not give it, shall be compelled to pay like a debtor and incur the first amercement.
By failing to take up what was promised and by withholding what has been given,
a mortal is born for a hundred million eons in the animal realm.
Where a gift is prescribed for the purpose of obtaining what has not yet been perceived,
that which is obtained through the act of perception is proclaimed as "wages" (bhṛti).
One should understand that what is obtained through this method for the sake of protection from fear, for the purpose of defense, or for the accomplishment of a task, constitutes a reciprocal favor.
"Even if it were said, 'I shall give my entire possessions to whoever delivers me from this life-threatening danger,' it would not necessarily come to pass."

That which is given by those who are not masters of themselves due to lust or anger, by the distressed, the weak, the insane, or the deluded, as well as that given through error or in jest, one may take back.
But as for a bribe that has been promised for the sake of accomplishing a task,
even if that object is accomplished, it must not be given under any circumstances.
If she has already been given away previously, he should be compelled to return her by force;
so say Gārgya and Mānava, that the fine shall be eleven times [the value].
Because of proclaiming thieves, violent criminals, the depraved, and adulterers;
because of seeing one whose livelihood has been ruined; and likewise because of practicing untruth.
Whatever has been obtained by these [mediators] is called a bribe;
in that case, the giver shall not be punished, but the mediator alone shall bear the guilt.
But if one who has been appointed to duties should receive a bribe,
he shall be made to pay that entire amount as well as a fine eleven times its value.
But if one who is not appointed should receive a bribe for the sake of the business,
there is no fault in him provided it is for the purpose of rendering a service in return.

Whether given by one who is healthy or by one who is afflicted, provided it was promised for the sake of dharma—if he dies without having given it, his son must be made to pay; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whatever has been mortgaged, sold, given, or received through fraud,
or whatever one perceives to have been acquired by means of deceit— that entire transaction one shall annul.
But when the wages are not fixed, the merchants, cowherds, and farmers shall receive a tenth part of the profit,
cattle, and crops, respectively.
[Non-payment of wages]:
But he who, having undertaken a work, does not have it completed even though it is possible, must be made to perform it by force; if he does not do so, he deserves punishment.
If the carrier causes an obstruction, he shall be made to pay double the wage for the journey.
But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by thieves, or destroyed by fire, or swept away by water.

He who abandons a companion on the road who is exhausted or afflicted by disease shall incur the first amercement; likewise, he who fails to provide protection for three days within a village shall incur the same.
But when that merchandise is lost or stolen on the way,
he shall receive wages proportional to the distance already traveled.
He who, having taken elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, camels, and so forth on lease,
does not return them after his purpose has been accomplished, shall be made to pay the lease along with a fine.

If one takes a house, a field, a shop, or other property on lease and does not return it to the owner, he shall be made to pay the value of the property along with the rent for as long as he has withheld it.
[Disputes between Owner and Herdsman]:
Bṛhaspati states that for animals entering fields, groves, pastures, houses, or cattle-pens, there shall be their seizure or beating.
In cases where the owner disputes the beating of animals— whether they be of low, high, or middle quality—
the king shall determine the appropriate punishment in that instance.
One should erect a great enclosure even before the crops have grown;
for deer, having once tasted their sweet flavor, are driven away here with great difficulty.
One should cause a quarter-pana to be paid for a cow, two quarters for a buffalo,
and likewise, a quarter is proclaimed as the fine for goats, sheep, and calves.
Neither the violation of a commitment nor the transgression of an agreement [is permissible];
rather, those who belong to a community should always perform all their duties according to the law of that community, remaining established in their own respective laws.
The royal decree has issued in accordance with the Dharma;
therefore, its practice must first be carried out by the king's command.
That man who does not observe the laws set forth by the king is blameworthy and wicked; he deserves punishment for violating the royal decree.
He who destroys what is logically consistent, he who provides no opportunity for the speaker,
and he who speaks what is illogical, shall be made to pay the first amercement.
The impetuous, the sower of dissension, and the destroyer of the community's property—all these must be executed after being publicly proclaimed as such before the king; thus said Bhṛgu.
Furthermore, whoever eats from the same vessel or in the same row as another,
if he does not act accordingly by pointing out that person's fault, he shall be punished.
Whatever debt may have been incurred on behalf of the community,
whether it was consumed or utilized for personal purposes, that must be paid by those very individuals.
Those who have attained the status of members in the midst of guilds, corporations,
or assemblies shall all receive equal shares of the previous wealth or debts.
In the same way, regarding the distribution of food and the performance of the duty of giving,
one who remains within the group shall share in the portion, but one who has departed shall not share in the portion.
Whatever has been acquired or preserved by them for the sake of the community, or whatever debt has been incurred,
as well as what was obtained through royal favor— all that belongs equally to everyone.
[The definitions of the designations such as *naigama* and others:
A *naigama* is proclaimed to be a collection of various citizens;
those who have assembled, bearing various weapons, are proclaimed to be *vrātas*.
A multitude of merchants and the like is proclaimed to be a *pūga*;
those who have settled into the life of renunciation are proclaimed to be *pāṣaṇḍas*.
A collection of Brāhmaṇas is proclaimed to be a *gaṇa*;
those who subsist by means of crafts are proclaimed to be artisans (*śilpin*).
The assembly of Arhats and followers of the Sugata is called a *saṅgha*;
the assembly of Cāṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and others is called a *gulma*.
Ganas, heretics, guilds, as well as corporations, trade unions, and whatever other assemblies exist that are termed "groups," Bṛhaspati says these are [the subjects of] the king.
[Regarding disputes over purchase and sale: Having purchased or sold, or having delivered [the goods],
if one who has bought [an item] does not accept it after having obtained it, or if one does not give back an undamaged item that was sold,
he shall recover his own property by paying a tenth part of the price.
If the time for the performance of the purposeful action has not arrived, one should certainly not cause it to be performed;
such is the rule within ten days, but beyond that, there is no further obligation.
In the case of land, the impurity lasts for ten days for both the seller and the buyer;
for the sapinda relatives, it lasts twelve days, and after that, it is minimal.
If a person, having purchased a commodity such as a milch cow or the like, should abandon it while still possessing a lingering desire for it,
provided the item is not defective and he returns it at the proper time, he shall pay a tenth part of the price.
If a buyer, having purchased [an item], departs with regret once it has come into his hand,
a wise person should abandon what was bought by paying one-sixth of its value there.
But that which was purchased without being examined, and later found to be defective, must be returned to the owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned.
But he who, having shown a faultless item, delivers one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double its price and undergo the same fine for misconduct.
If the merchandise should be damaged, burnt, or stolen,
that loss belongs solely to the seller who, having sold it, does not deliver it.
If a buyer does not accept goods being offered for sale,
or if a seller sells elsewhere what has already been sold, neither of them shall be held at fault.

If something is sold for a low price by one who is intoxicated, or out of fear, or by one who is not his own master, or by one who is deluded, it must be relinquished; it shall belong to him once again.
One should examine [the quality] of milk for three days, or indeed for five days;
however, for pearls, diamonds, and corals, the examination should last for seven days.
For bipeds, the period is half a month for males, but double that for females;
for all seeds it is ten days, and for metals and clothes it is one day.
If, however, a defect in the merchandise should arise before that time,
it must be returned by the seller, and the buyer shall recover the purchase price.
However, a garment that has been worn, which is soiled, stained,
and even defective, once purchased, shall not be returned by the seller.
But that which has been purchased as common property, the lowest of men should not give it away alone;
he should not take it, nor should he accept it, nor indeed should he sell it.
If a purchaser, having bought a commodity for a price, considers it a bad purchase,
it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it has not been examined.
On the second day, the purchaser giving it back shall take one-third of the price as compensation;
on the third day, twice that amount; after that, it belongs to the purchaser alone.
Having divided the value of the goods into five parts, three parts are called the price;
the fourth part is the profit, and the fifth is said to be the true [value].
Whether through a joint, an exchange, or an unequal transaction involving the three types of enjoyment,
or even by command or purchase, one may rescind the sale within ten years.
It is the settled conclusion that even the practice of buying and selling land does not exist for those who have not obtained permission from their kinsmen and others who are nearby and blameless.
In one's own village, it shall be ten nights; in another village, three fortnights;
in other kingdoms, six months; but when there is a difference in dialect, it shall be one year.
But when the tax-payer has fled,
the members of the court shall sell the tax-paying land for the sake of the tax, together with the surety for the tax.
But by neighboring lords who are assembled together, who are knowledgeable, and who fear wrongdoing,
[the boundaries] of fields, groves, houses, and so forth, as well as of bipeds and quadrupeds, [should be determined].
They say that the price is "determined" after dividing it into eight parts;
if it exceeds one part or falls short, it is considered improper.
Even after a hundred years have passed, all of that is revoked;
whatever price a commodity rightfully deserves in a sale or purchase, that is what must be paid according to dharma.
If, when the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, or even the eighth part has elapsed,
the purchase and sale have been concluded, [the following applies].
All that which is of inferior value, even if completed, shall be as if uncompleted;
when the price is lower than what was stated, the purchase is not at all vitiated.
By that very fraction, it would be diminished in value in purchase or sale;
other people who know the law say that even such a case is "unexecuted."
A purchase is successful when the price is half more than the standard; a profit exceeding ten percent is as stated.
A lease may be made with a one-third share, and a sale by mutual consent may be concluded immediately.
Even if only a small amount is given from the price, the purchase shall be considered completed;
in the case of compound interest (cakravṛddhi), that which is to be paid must be given even without a formal agreement.

[Failure to serve after having agreed: But he who, having accepted [the pupil], does not teach the craft and instead makes him perform other tasks, shall incur the first amercement; from that, the pupil withdraws.
Even if he has been trained, a pupil may practice his desire for worldly gain;
whatever work he performs therein, the fruit of that belongs to the teacher alone.
Bhṛgu maintains that by giving away one's own independent self, one enters a state of servitude similar to that of a wife;
however, this servitude is to be understood as applying to the three [lower] castes, and never to a Brāhmaṇa.
Servitude exists according to the direct order of the castes, not in the inverse order;
for the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras lose their independence [by serving those below them].
Even if he is of the same caste, one must never compel a Brahmin to servitude;
for by the servitude of a Brahmin, O King, the royal majesty is destroyed.

But Bṛhaspati has declared that a Brāhmaṇa should never, under any circumstances, be made to perform the duties of a slave or the occupations of a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra among those of equal caste.

Even toward one who is endowed with virtue and Vedic study, the best of the twice-born should not intentionally perform any action that falls short of what is due; nor should he do anything unwholesome in that regard.
The cleansing of feces and urine, as well as massaging while naked,
and the tending of cattle and other such tasks— these are generally performed by the sons of female slaves.
In a place where the three castes, beginning with the twice-born, have abandoned the life of renunciation,
the king should impose exile upon the Brāhmaṇa and slavery upon the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya.
But a Śūdra, whether bought or even unbought, one should make a slave;
for he was created by the Self-existent One himself solely for servitude.
If one should have sexual intercourse with his own female slave and she should subsequently give birth, then,
having considered the seed [of the father], that woman along with her offspring shall not remain a slave.
Whatever wealth a slave may possess, it is traditionally held that the master is its lord;
however, as for property acquired through open sale, the master does not deserve that wealth.
A female slave who is married by a slave shall also attain the status of a slave;
for her husband is her master, and since the master is dependent upon his own owner.
If anyone should take a Brāhmaṇī woman as a wife, or likewise purchase her, that act is considered invalid by the king; all of them should be punished.

But he who, out of lust, should make a woman of good family a slave by force, or should transfer her to another, shall be punished; and that [marriage] shall be considered as never having been performed.
He who enjoys the care of a nurse or a non-servant woman as if she were a slave,
or the wife of an attendant, shall incur the first amercement.
He who, being capable and not in a state of distress, desires to sell a devoted female slave who is crying out [in protest], shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
And he who, being dependent, offers himself [to another] saying, "I am yours," shall not obtain that desired object; the former owner shall regain him.
A slave who has been ordained as a renunciant must not be released by anyone;
however, one who has been maintained [as a slave] during a time of distress is freed from slavery by giving a pair of oxen.
[Disputes concerning boundaries: Excess, deficiency, and partiality; existence and non-existence;
non-enjoyment, possession, and the boundary—these six are the causes for disputes over land.
In that case, the enjoyment [of the property] must be applied while all witnesses remain present;
for a witness may be either one recorded in writing or another who follows the two paths [of oral testimony].
In disputes between two parties concerning fields, buildings, tanks, wells, groves, or embankments, as well as in all other matters, the neighbors are the authoritative witnesses.
In the case of neighboring lands, one should determine the boundaries of fields and so forth with those who are not neighbors;
likewise, this applies to village boundaries, as well as to cities and districts.
A village is declared to be the neighbor of a village; a field is the neighbor of a field;
and a house is specified as the neighbor of a house, for it indeed encircles them on all sides.
In their absence, neighbors, hereditary tenants, elders, those who have been evicted, and so forth [should be examined];
this applies even to the six types of immovable property—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
When the neighboring kings are engaged in battle, and those further beyond them are likewise engaged,
and those who are engaged with those already engaged are also joined, this formation is proclaimed as the "Lotus" (padmākāra).
When neighboring vassals have become corrupt in the pursuit of their own interests due to the weight of material gain, their extraction must be carried out by those associated with them;
there is no doubt in this matter.
But those who are attached to those who are themselves attached and corrupted by faults are declared to be "associated with them";
however, a king who understands the Dharma should not punish those who are not actually corrupt.
For neighboring lords are not released from liability regarding a decision simply by claiming ignorance;
if they declare ignorance, they should be fined and the boundary should be investigated again.
If a dispute should arise after [the boundary] has been proclaimed, they shall be punished with the highest fine.
Having dismissed wicked neighboring lords, he should cause the boundary to be established together with other hereditary officials and others; thus do those who know the Dharma understand it.
Those who were formerly neighbors there but later went to another country are proclaimed by the sages as "original" (maula) because they are rooted in that very place.
Those endowed with human virtues who have witnessed the task being accomplished—
whether they be old or not old— are proclaimed as "the elders."
Because they extract [beings] from that [state] by means of eavesdropping, enjoyment, performing tasks, and giving explanations,
they are therefore known as "Uddhṛtas" (the Extracted).
The neighboring kings are considered to possess one unit of quality when they state what is undesirable at the outset;
those who respond with twice that quality are known as the "superior" (uttara); others beyond them are held to possess three units of quality.
Just as one who is desired by both parties might lead them to a boundary somewhere, placing earth upon his head, clad in red garments, and composed in mind; so too [should the witness act].
It was composed by King Bhayavarjita himself when all [other teachers] were absent.
And [this applies] to fields, wells, and tanks, as well as to rice-paddies and groves,
and to houses, palaces, dwellings, royal residences, and temples of the gods.
But if, among those many who have been summoned, they do not reach a decision because of fear or greed, they shall be made to pay the highest fine.
In the case of crossing a boundary, in a treasury, and likewise upon touching with the foot,
it is prescribed that [the period of purification] lasts for three fortnights, one fortnight, and seven days, depending on whether the cause was divine or royal.
One should not obstruct the girdle-closet, the window, or the air-hole; nor should one block the drain or the site of the house, for by so doing, one becomes liable to a fine.
After the time of settling [the house], these [rites] should never be performed again;
one should not cast a glance or create a water-channel toward another's dwelling.
One should construct dwellings with a rampart of excrement, urine, and water, containing fire-pits and chasms;
leaving a space of two cubits, one should build against the walls of others.
That which all people always traverse is a crossroads;
that royal road is called "unobstructed" as long as it remains open at the proper time.
One should not plant anything there, nor should one damage it in any way;
however, by obstructing the path of the preceptor, the teacher, the king, and others, one incurs punishment.
If anyone there should out of desire discharge excrement into the refuse heaps, pits, or even plant trees, his fine shall be one māṣaka.
He who destroys tanks, gardens,
or sacred bathing places with impure matter shall first have that impurity cleared away and then be fined the first amercement.
One who defiles established holy fords (tīrtha) set up by great-souled ones—
those which are meritorious and purifying— shall incur the punishment for the first degree of violence.
But for trees grown within the boundary line between two fields,
one should declare that their fruits and flowers belong in common to the owners of both fields.
But for those born in another's field whose branches are supported elsewhere,
one should know him to be the owner in whose fields they are supported.
But he who performs a renovation of a house, a garden, or a tank without the consent of the owner does not obtain [ownership] of that renovated property.
If an expenditure has been incurred when the master has arrived and it was not reported to the king,
yet it is subsequently reported and authorized, then [the servant] receives that expenditure as being for his own account.
If he does not pay because of incapacity,
then the cultivator shall receive the fruit of the crop minus one-eighth, which represents the expenses incurred for the fallow land;
he shall be the enjoyer for eight years, but after that, it belongs to the owner.
If someone should cultivate a field that belongs to an owner who is incapable, deceased, or lost, he shall enjoy its fruit without being hindered.
If a field is being drawn for cultivation, the original owner may return;
having provided all the labor and maintenance, he shall regain possession of that field.
Then, by a reduction of one-eighth each year until seven years have passed,
at the completion of the eighth year, he shall obtain the field that has been enjoyed.
[Harsh speech: To mimic or to utter sounds such as "hum," coughing, or whatever else is censured in the world—
that is called harsh speech.
Because of its harshness, vulgarity, and severity, that [abuse] is also recorded as being threefold:
censure is to be known as harsh; what is designated as a physical defect is vulgar;
and the wise say that severity consists of insults involving acts leading to loss of caste.
When one, by means of limbs characterized as unreal— whether they be non-existent or even existent— insults another,
that is known by the wise as harsh speech.
When one, out of anger, uses speech to cause the humiliation of another's conduct,
country, family, and so forth, that is considered by the wise to be *aślīlā* (obscene).
That speech which binds one with the noose of great sins, which produces passion and hatred, or which causes the loss of caste, is known as "intense" (tīvra).

Those who, out of anger, proclaim the faults of others, or being themselves devoid of virtue, pretend to recognize virtue in them, or who are preoccupied with false notions— such a man they know to be corrupt in speech.
Those who proclaim the faults of one who is actually faultless for the sake of finding fault,
and who speaks using pretexts, such a man they know as one whose speech is corrupt.
Whatever has been spoken by me out of delusion, negligence, rivalry, or even out of affection,
saying "I shall not speak thus again"— for that, one should prescribe half the penalty.
Where there might be a mention by him of one who has fallen [from his caste] for the sake of a rebuttal,
there would be no fault on account of that statement, provided he can demonstrate it.
Otherwise, there would be an equal fault; however, in the case of speaking falsely, it is recorded as the highest [offense].
One should purify a person corrupted by speech through a great vow of application.
The king should investigate with diligence any matter reported that is untrue;
for those whose habit is to speak falsehoods, the cutting off of the tongue is the means of purification.
[Regarding assault:
If one cannot perceive the grounds for assault through witnesses and other means,
one should employ evidence provided by witnesses or even divine ordeals in that case.
That man who strikes with a terrifying weapon,
whether he himself has been previously oppressed or not, is declared to be deserving of punishment.
According to Bhṛgu, for the cutting off of the ears, lips, nose, feet, eyes, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine is prescribed; for the piercing [of these], the middle fine.
When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the sake of causing pain,
the punishment should be inflicted in exact proportion to the suffering that has been caused.
For those who are untouchable, for rogues, slaves, barbarians, evildoers,
and those born of inverse unions, beating is not a punishment intended to serve a purpose.
That [water] becomes fourfold when mixed with vomit, urine, feces, and so forth;
it is known to become sixfold within the body, but eightfold at the head.
For raising the hand [to strike], a fine of twelve [paṇas] shall be imposed;
for actually striking those of one's own caste, that same fine is declared to be double.
Just as the punishments for verbal abuse have been declared according to the inverse and direct order [of the castes],
so too shall the punishments be inflicted in due order for physical assault.
But when the body or the sense organs are destroyed,
the wise should impose a fine and likewise provide that which brings satisfaction as well as the means for recovery; he shall bear the expenses of recovery until the wound is healed.

Those offenders against whom verbal censure or physical beating has been prescribed must be made to restore what was stolen or broken; however, those who possess no wealth shall be purified through labor.
If a man yokes animals such as donkeys, cows, buffaloes, or camels when they are exhausted, afflicted by thirst, hungry, or at an improper time, he shall incur the first amercement.
For the killing of wild animals or birds, the fine shall be twelve paṇas;
for the killing of snakes, cats, mongooses, dogs, or pigs by men, it shall be two paṇas.

One who drives a cow, a young heifer, a sacrificial animal, a castrated bull, or a full-grown bull [for sport] shall first incur a fine of one thousand panas, and for such an act, the ultimate punishment is death.
In the case of killing living beings,
Manu has declared that one should give a substitute for them, or pay a value corresponding to that [loss].
It is the settled rule that the punishment for injuring any of the forest trees should be applied in proportion to their utility.
If a teacher should strike a disciple out of anger without using a cane,
such that excessive pain is caused, there would be a dispute between the disciple and the father-like teacher.
[Impetuous action]: That deed which is performed impulsively is declared to be *sāhasa*.
Theft is defined as taking away with the knowledge of the owner, as well as forcible seizure; likewise, it constitutes violence (sāhasa), while its concealment is called denial (vinihnava).
But when a legal matter proceeds without marks [of guilt] and is termed a rash act (*sāhasa*), it shall be cleared by means of oaths; this is the rule in all such cases.
If many enraged men should kill a single person,
he among them who strikes the vital organ is traditionally considered the slayer.
One who commits such an act through malice shall incur various forms of execution;
however, one should indeed kill without hesitation an approaching person who intends to cause destruction.
There is no fault for the slayer of evildoers who have risen up [to commit harm];
however, when they have desisted from their undertaking, their seizure is not considered a killing.

In the case of an assailant who is superior by virtue of asceticism, Vedic study, or birth, there should be no killing; however, Bhṛgu maintains that killing is permissible for one who is inferior in merit.
One who brandishes a sword, poison, or fire; likewise one who holds a bow raised in his hand;
one who kills by means of the Atharvaveda; and one who is treacherous toward the king.
One who violates his wife and one who is intent on seeking out his vulnerabilities—
one should recognize all such persons as *ātatāyin*s (assassins).
They say that those who steal one's reputation or conduct, and those who seize one's dharma or wealth, are evil men.
But one who commits an offense against someone who has never previously been accused,
or who seizes one's life or property— one should know him to be an *ātatāyin* (an assailant).
In the killing of those with claws, those with horns, those with fangs, or assassins,
as well as elephants, horses, and others, the slayer incurs no guilt.
One who causes an abortion is a thief; likewise, even a Brāhmaṇa, having killed an innocent woman, must be put to death by the stroke of a weapon.
A man who causes injury, breakage, or crushing of goods shall be liable for the first amercement; the owner of the goods is declared to be the one who receives compensation.
If one should carry off, break, or burn an image of the gods,
or likewise destroy its temple, he shall incur the first amercement.
He who should breach a wall, cause it to fall, or likewise demolish it,
or block the course of water, shall incur the first amercement.
Whether it be concealed or open, by night or by day,
the taking of another's property is proclaimed to be theft.
One should carefully examine any stolen property that has fallen from another's hand, been picked up on the ground unintentionally, or dropped by a thief.
One who acts by means of scales, measures, weights, or counterfeit articles,
whether openly or secretly, shall incur the first amercement.
If something is stolen from a house, however, the king shall cause the thieves to be seized; and if the thief is not found, he shall make the guards and the local officials pay for it.
Property stolen from within a village shall be made good by the village headman;
in a pasture, it shall be given by the owner; and in a royal preserve, it shall be restored by the one who recovers the thief.
Whatever has been kept by anyone in his own country must be given back by the king;
the monarch himself should recover and take possession of what was lost and subsequently found.
If goods have been stolen by thieves, the king should diligently restore their original form;
in its absence, however, there should be payment of its value, otherwise the king becomes a sinner.
Even if the thief has been caught, if the stolen property cannot be recovered from him,
one should either surrender that thief or cause him to be surrendered at will.
If, however, there should be doubt regarding the guilt of those being compelled to pay,
the one who was robbed shall be made to take an oath, or he may be cleared by his kinsmen.
Since the owner has recovered only a small portion of the property taken away,
he shall receive that remainder once the owner has made his claim.
Those who would strike at their own country, as well as those who obstruct the royal highways— the king, having confiscated all their property, shall impale them upon a stake.
Property recovered by those intent on searching for thieves shall be made over to the thiefless owner;
in that case, the king should cause double that amount to be paid as a reward.
With whichever limb a thief commits an injury against another,
the king shall cut off that very limb, so that he does not do it again.
Taking two each of cucumber and gourd, five mangoes, five pomegranates, and a handful of dates, jujubes, and so forth, one does not incur fault.
Mānavas say that the immediate banishment of those caught in adultery is what Gautamas find undesirable, as it is censurable because it results in the destruction of living beings.
Whether the act was committed in the presence of witnesses or not,
once the perpetrator has been apprehended and his violent crime established through evidence, he shall be punished by confiscation of all his property after being formally charged.
But those who are bound with iron chains, though they may have meager rations, if they are endowed with strength, shall perform the king's tasks until death; so says Kauśika.
When property has been brought from a foreign land by a foreigner,
having seized that property, he should release him without punishment.
Those who provide food for thieves, as well as those who supply fire and water,
those who purchase their goods, those who accept them,
and those who conceal them— all these are declared by the law to be subject to the same punishment.
If there should be an ignorant officiating priest or an unstable teacher,
the king, having punished both of them with the penalty prescribed for a thief, should establish them on the right path.
[Adultery with a woman:
If he employs a female messenger, stays at an improper time or place,
or seizes her by the throat, hair, or moving limbs, or by the ear, nose, hand, and so forth;
Staying in one place, sitting, and moderation in food—this is known as the ninefold gathering.
When a man forcibly indulges in sexual intercourse with women, he should proceed to kill him; for that is a transgression of duty.
But a wanton woman who, afflicted by lust, desires him of her own accord,
shall be released by the king's command after being publicly proclaimed in the presence of the people.
The initiator, the accomplice, the instructor of the path,
the refuge, the provider of weapons, and the provider of food to those who perform evil deeds.
One who instructs in war, one who demonstrates its destruction,
one who is intent on indifference toward what ought to be done, and one who approves of faults through speech.
If there should be those who are unable to prevent [the offense], all of them must perform that task;
however, one should impose upon them a punishment proportionate to their respective capacities.
[The Duties of Wife and Husband: A wife, not separated from her husband, should serve the sacred fire with humility,
desiring good fortune and freedom from widowhood through devotion to her husband.
By means of devotion to her husband alone, a woman attains all desires;
returning here from heaven, she becomes a treasury of happiness.
A virtuous woman who, upon the death of her husband,
remains established in celibacy and conducts herself like Arundhatī, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
[The Division of Inheritance: When the father and the brothers take the entire collection of property in equal shares, that is declared to be the righteous division.
The paternal estate is common to both the father and the son;
however, in property acquired by the father himself, the son does not possess ownership.
Whatever was inherited from the grandfather, whatever was inherited from the father, and whatever else was acquired by oneself—
all this is divided when there is a partition among the heirs.
When there is suspicion of hidden property, visible items such as a house, a field, or a quadruped may be divided; in that case, it is declared that the means of proof lies therein.
Household utensils, draft animals, milch cattle, ornaments, and those engaged in manual labor are divided while being visible; regarding hidden property, Bhṛgu declared that it goes to the treasury.
Upon the division of property during one's lifetime, a father shall not favor one son over another;
nor shall he disinherit a single son without cause or reason.
And the partition [of the estate] is ordained for those who have attained legal capacity;
for men, the status of being legally competent arises at the sixteenth year.
And the wealth of those who have not yet attained legal capacity,
as well as that of those who have gone abroad, shall be deposited with kinsmen and friends, free from any expenditure.
All [the heirs] together shall protect the share of one who has gone abroad;
when a son dies while still a child, his inheritance must be protected by his maternal relatives (tantubandhu);
once he has reached the age of puberty (paugaṇḍa), they shall divide it according to their respective shares.
A debt contracted by a brother, a paternal uncle, or a mother for the sake of the family must be paid in its entirety by the heirs at the time of partition.
That debt must be paid to the creditor; one should not cause it to be paid otherwise.
If it has been proven by evidence, then [the claim] is barred by contradiction.

A debt contracted for the sake of dharma, or one given out of affection, or that which was incurred through employment—such a debt should be divided while it is still visible; it is not a gift from the paternal estate.

A debt of this kind— whether inherited from a father and cleared of the paternal debt, or one's own personal debt contracted by oneself— must be settled by the kinsmen together during the partition of the estate.
Having paid off debts and provided for those who bestow affection, one should divide the remainder.
Before the son has acquired property, the father shall take two shares or half;
when the father has died, the mother also receives a share equal to that of a son.
In whatever manner the wealth obtained through partition may be brought to serve the purpose of sacrifice,
in that same manner the learned should ensure the honor due to the shares.
Even in the division of inheritance in this world, no one shall attain ownership;
rather, only enjoyment may be exercised, but neither giving nor selling is permitted.
Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights regarding immovable property;
for an individual has no power over any of it in matters of gift, mortgage, or sale.
If a younger brother dies before the property has been divided, one should provide for his son with an inheritance such that he receives nothing from the grandfather.
He shall receive his paternal share from his uncle or from that uncle’s son;
for that same share rightfully belongs to all brothers.
His son may also receive it, but beyond him there should be cessation [of inheritance].
When a legitimate son has been born, sons of the same caste (savarṇa) shall receive a fourth part of the inheritance;
however, those of a different caste (asavarṇa) are entitled only to food and clothing.
For unmarried daughters, however, a fourth part is prescribed;
for sons, there are three parts, but equality is ordained when the wealth is small.
If one should produce fruit even with the consent of the landowner, both of them are sharers of that fruit here in this world; for indeed, there is no fruit without one [of the two].
If a woman, having abandoned a eunuch or an outcast husband, takes another husband,
the son born of her from that second husband is clearly the offspring of the biological progenitor.
He whose urine is not frothy and whose feces sink in water,
and who lacks the penis, insanity, and semen— he is called a *klība* (impotent).
Furthermore, the son born of a woman married out of order, one born of a woman of the same lineage (sagotra),
and one who has fallen from the religious life— none of these are entitled to inherit property.
But the son of a woman married out of order inherits the estate if he is of the same caste as his father;
so too does the son born of a woman of a different caste who was married in the proper order.
The son of a woman born in the inverse order of castes does not inherit property;
it is held that his kinsmen should provide him with food and clothing for as long as he lives.
In the absence even of kinsmen, he shall obtain that paternal property;
however, kinsmen should not be compelled to pay property that is not ancestral.
[The following are] indivisible:
that which was taken away by one's own power, that which was lost, and that which was acquired by oneself;
all this is not to be given by the father to his sons at the time of partition.
Whatever wealth has been acquired through that knowledge which was obtained by means of consuming food provided by another,
that is called "wealth acquired through knowledge" (vidyāprāpta).
But that which is obtained through learning after it has been offered as a wager, one should know to be "learning-wealth" (vidyādhanam); it is not to be divided in a partition.

That which is obtained from a pupil, from officiating as a priest, from answering questions, from resolving doubts through inquiry, from praising one's own knowledge, from debate, and from recitation—
this they call the "wealth of learning," and it is not to be divided during partition.
For this same rule applies even to artisans regarding whatever may be in excess of the agreed price.

Bṛhaspati states that what is obtained through learning after having set aside [other means], such as by means of gambling, should be known as "wealth acquired through learning" (vidyādhanam); it is not to be divided.

That which is obtained through a promise for instruction, that which is received from a pupil, and that which is obtained according to the rule of the officiating priest (ṛtvij)— Bhṛgu declares this to be the wealth acquired through learning.

That which is acquired through the power of learning, as well as from officiating at sacrifices or from teaching students—this they call "wealth of learning"; anything other than this is common property.
Bṛhaspati states that wealth acquired through valor by brothers who have been trained in the sciences within the family, or even by their father, is subject to partition.
A physician should never give away any portion of his medical wealth to those who are ignorant;
however, he may give that wealth to those whose knowledge is equal to or superior to his own.
When one performs an action having boldly entered into uncertainty,
