and the master, being pleased with that action, bestows his favor,
whatever wealth is obtained therein through valor shall belong to him.
That which is acquired through valor, that which is obtained through learning, and that which is traditionally declared to be a woman's property—
all this must not be divided by the heirs during a partition.
That which is acquired by means of a banner (dhvajāhṛta) is declared not to be subject to division;
that which is brought back from battle after routing the enemy force,
having sacrificed one's life for the sake of the master, is called "acquired by means of a banner."
Whatever is obtained at the time of giving along with a maiden of one's own caste—
that wealth situated in the maiden is declared to be pure and productive of increase.
One should know that wealth brought by a wife at the time of marriage is matrimonial; all such property is to be understood as conducive to the fulfillment of dharma.
Whatever is given to the bride at the time of marriage,
intended for the groom, all that wealth belongs to her and is not to be divided by her kinsmen.
But wealth recorded in documents, that which was designated for religious purposes, water, a slave, and any hereditary pledge; K_882 //
Clothing and ornaments that may not be appropriate should be set aside;
rather, kinsmen should provide such things as are suitable for the occasion.
Bṛhaspati declares that pasture land for cattle, protection, clothing, and whatever is attached to the body should not be divided, but used [in common] for the sake of dharma.
Whatever law has been declared for a country, a caste, a guild, or a village,
by that very law one should determine the distribution of inheritance.
[The Division of Concealed Property: If property that was concealed is later discovered, it shall be divided equally with the brothers; indeed, in the absence of the father, the sons shall divide it.
Whatever property may have been withheld from one another or improperly divided, if it is recovered later, it should be divided into equal shares; so says Bhṛgu.
Whatever wealth is obtained by one who has already divided [the inheritance] shall belong to him alone;
however, what was seized, lost, or subsequently found, as well as what was previously mentioned, shall be shared again.
One must not cause property seized by a relative to be returned by force;
nor should one cause the enjoyment of property belonging to undivided relatives to be restored [to a claimant].
Having abandoned the common field and settled in another country,
a share must undoubtedly be given to a descendant of that family who returns.
Whether it be the third, the fifth, or even the seventh [birth],
if the births are not fully known, one shall receive the portion that has come down in succession.

The land acquired by those born of the same lineage should be given to one who has come from that family, provided that the primary and neighboring lords have traditionally recognized him as their master.
If those who were divided from the paternal estate are living together again, they should divide it once more; he shall receive two shares from which his prosperity arose.
Those brothers who live for ten years with distinct marks and so forth, having separate religious duties and separate activities,
should be known as divided from the paternal wealth.

[The characteristics of women’s property and the types of women’s property: That which is received before the fire, that which is received at the wedding procession, that which is given out of affection by her [relatives],
and that which is obtained from her brothers, mother, or father— this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.
That which is given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is proclaimed by the virtuous as *adhyagnika* (fire-acquired) woman's property.
Furthermore, whatever a woman receives while being led away from her father's house,
as well as the *adhyāvahanika*, is declared to be her *strīdhana* (woman’s property).
Whatever is given out of affection by a mother-in-law or a father-in-law,
as well as that which is given upon the salutation of their feet, is called "affectionately given" (prītidatta).
Whatever price is obtained for household utensils, vehicles, milch animals, ornaments, or articles for manual labor— that is proclaimed as *śulka*.
Whatever is obtained by a woman from her husband's family after marriage is called *anvādheya*, as is what is obtained from her own [maternal] kin.

Whatever has been obtained after marriage from her husband, from her parents, or from her father-in-law, whether through formal gift (saṃskāra), out of affection, or as a subsequent gift (anvādheya)— that, according to Bhṛgu, is [the woman's property].
Whether by a married woman or by an unmarried girl, what is obtained from her husband, from her father’s house,
from her brother, or from her parents, is declared to be *saudāyika* (a woman's separate property).
[Consideration of Ownership and Other Matters Regarding Women’s Property:

Women’s property (strīdhana) should be given to a woman by her father, mother, husband, brother, or paternal kinsmen, according to their ability, up to a maximum of two thousand [paṇas], with the exception of immovable property. K. 902.
However, that which is given with a specific condition, or that which is given through the influence of a connection by the father, brother, or husband, is not intended to be "woman's property."

Whatever wealth has been acquired through crafts, or whatever else has been obtained through affection from others, the husband’s ownership extends over that; the remainder, however, is declared to be the woman's property.
Upon receiving her dowry, independence is prescribed for women,
because that was given by their [relatives] as a means of subsistence out of compassion.
It is declared that women always possess independence over their *saudāyika* (dowry) property;
they may sell or give it away as they wish, even in the case of immovable assets.
Upon the death of her husband, a woman may dispose of her husband’s inheritance as she pleases;
however, while he is still living, she must preserve it, otherwise it shall be forfeited to his family.
But if he has two wives and does not favor her again,
even if she was given [to him] out of affection, he must be compelled by force to restore her.
Wherever a woman is deprived of food, clothing, and shelter,
she may take for herself her own property, as well as a share from the heirs.
This is the law for one who has been written [in a will]: she shall reside in the husband's family when it is reached;
but if she is ill, she may go to her kinsmen at the time of his death.
Neither the husband, nor the son, nor the father, nor the brothers have authority over the woman's property,
whether in its acquisition or its disposal.
For if even one among these should forcibly consume the woman's property,
he shall be made to pay it back with interest and shall also incur a fine.
If one should eat that very same thing after having obtained permission and with a sense of pleasure,
he should be made to pay its price, provided that he is wealthy.
Having learned that [the debtor] is diseased, in distress, or oppressed by creditors, he may,
out of affection and by his own will, give what has been relinquished [to him].
While she is alive, her husband, sons, brothers-in-law, paternal kinsmen, and maternal relatives are declared to have no power over her property; those who seize it are liable to punishment.
The sons must repay the woman's property as a debt, just as they would what was promised by her husband;
she who remains in the husband's family shall not dwell in her father's family.
The sisters, together with their husbands and kinsmen, shall divide the property of a deceased woman;
this is the law regarding a woman’s wealth, and thus the division has been ordained.
In the absence of daughters, however, that inheritance shall go to the sons;
but property given by kinsmen goes to the kinsmen, and in their absence, it goes to the husband.
Furthermore, whatever immovable property has been given by both parents to a daughter always goes to her brothers upon her death, provided she leaves no offspring.
Whatever paternal property a woman has acquired from her father-in-law and others,
it is ordained that in the absence of her offspring, it belongs to her mother and father.

[On the inheritance of the property of one who dies without a son: A wife who has no son, remaining with her elders and preserving the bed of her husband, shall enjoy it until death with patience; after that, the heirs shall take possession. K. 921.
When the husband has gone to heaven, the wife, however, is entitled to food and clothing;
but if the share of the wealth has not been divided, she receives it until the end of her life.
She who is devoted to serving her teacher deserves to enjoy her allotted share;
if she does not perform service, she should be employed in [menial tasks such as] weaving cloth and gathering alms-food.
Upon the death of her husband, a woman who protects her family may receive her husband's share;
however, as long as he lives, she has no ownership over it for the purposes of giving, mortgaging, or selling.
One who is devoted to vows and fasting, established in celibacy,
and constantly delighting in self-restraint and generosity, shall go to heaven even if she is childless.
The wife who is unfaithful to her husband shall be the taker of his wealth;
in her absence, however, it shall be the daughter, provided she be unmarried.
Now, for one who has no son, a wife of noble birth or even daughters [are designated];
in their absence, the father, mother, brother, and sons are declared [to be the heirs].
When [the estate] has been partitioned and settled, in the absence of a son, the father shall take the property;
or the brother, or the mother, or the father’s mother, in that order.
[But those women who are] addicted to misconduct, shameless, or wasteful of wealth [shall not receive it].
And a woman who is devoted to adultery does not deserve that wealth.
If a woman performs funeral rites for the deceased without being authorized by her father, husband, or son,
that act of hers shall be fruitless.
Property that has no heir goes to the king, as do the funeral expenses for a wife or a slave;
however, setting aside the property of a *śrotriya*, one should bestow that upon other *śrotriyas*.
Those who are united [in marriage] shall inherit from those united; those who live separately, from those living separately.
In the absence [of heirs], they should be known as the takers of the property; those without seed [or offspring] share with one another.
[Regarding gambling and betting: One should never indulge in gambling, which increases anger and greed,
produces wicked people, is cruel, and destroys the wealth of men.
Since strife inevitably arises from gambling, just as venom from the mouth of a serpent,
therefore a king should desist from it, for that is indeed a vice regarding his domain.
If it should be visible, with a gateway and arch standing at the entrance,
one should have that *karapada* constructed for the sake of preventing the confusion of the noble ones.
The master of the gambling house shall conduct the game and personally pay the stake to the king;
he may take a ten percent interest from the winnings resulting from defeat.

The winner shall give his own wealth, and from the loser, the stake should be taken within three fortnights, or immediately by the keeper of the gambling house itself; there is no doubt regarding this matter.
Whether appearing as a single form or a double form, victory belongs to that gambler at dice upon whom protection is established.
Alternatively, a gambler who gives the king the share as prescribed may engage in gambling openly; in this way, no fault is found.
One should cause what is owed to be paid by force in that very place, and not otherwise;
for in that case, the one who has won is the master of the hall, and the legal proceeding depends upon the authority of the master of the hall.

One who is defeated while ignorant should be released; one who is defeated while knowledgeable should not be released. Even when everything has been won back and the opponent is made knowledgeable, one should not compel him to surrender his entire property.
In disputes over victory, gain, or the fraudulent methods of gamblers,
the master of the gaming hall is the authority, provided that the master of the hall is himself pure.
There is no certainty regarding the king for those who follow the conduct established by barbarians, outcastes, rogues, gamblers, and ascetics.

[The Miscellaneous Section: Whatever remains unsaid from what was previously stated, and whatever has fallen away from its proper context, having been extracted and composed for the sake of another treatise, is inconsistent.
That which stands as a restatement at the end of a treatise for the sake of illustration,
or that statement which follows this same method, shall be known as *prakīrṇaka* (a miscellaneous or supplementary utterance).
The duties of kings, one's own specific duties, the discussion of doubtful matters,
and whatever remains unsaid from what was previously mentioned— all that constitutes the miscellaneous section (prakīrṇaka).
The sixth-part tax and the toll should likewise be paid into the pit;
as well as those who cause dissension in battle or among thieves, and those who violate the wives of others.
The intent to kill cows or Brahmins, as well as the destruction of crops—
the king himself should investigate these ten offenses.

The failure to perform expiations, the transgression of prohibitions and injunctions, the destruction of the system of castes and stages of life, and the neglect of the prevention of the intermixture of castes.
A hidden treasure, wealth that yields no fruit, and the acquisition of riches by a pauper—
the king himself, having learned of these through his spies, should prevent them.
Those matters should not be discussed: the ritual actions of disputants, the provocation of the *prakṛtis*, and mutual secret signals.
Whatever among his subjects proceeds contrary to the injunctions of the scriptures,
the king should pacify these by means of the expedients of conciliation, sowing dissension, and so forth.
One should employ verbal punishment against friends and others, saying, "Shame on you, wretched woman!
One should do to him exactly what was said; even if it was not explicitly stated, one should act as if it were well-considered.
But whoever should accomplish a legal matter by means of a false measure, or by a forged seal or a counterfeit stamp, shall indeed be made to pay the highest fine.
Those who are addicted to royal amusements, those who subsist on the king's service,
and whoever speaks what is unpleasant— he should carry out their execution.
Those who manufacture counterfeit coins, those who examine them,
those who distribute them, and those who steal the king's wealth shall receive various forms of corporal punishment.

A Śūdra who has entered the life of a renunciant and is devoted to the recitation of prayers and burnt offerings, if he commits a sin, should be punished by execution; or else, he should be fined double the usual penalty.
Even if the crime is accompanied by clear evidence, one should inquire into the cause of the offense;
then, having carefully ascribed the fault, one should determine the punishment.
But when an offense occurs among all those of good conduct,
even if it happens involuntarily through fate, one should not impose punishment in that case.
Kings who administer punishment correctly are worthy of worship even by the gods.
At the commencement [of an offense], one should apply the lowest penalty; in its continuation, a middle penalty is prescribed.
Whatever punishment has been ordained for whom, that indeed shall be sufficient for him.
Kings and ministers especially shall attain such [merit] by not failing to punish the wicked and by inflicting punishment upon those who bow before them.
Those who are dependent on others, those who exist in a state of servitude, and those who are without a protector are designated as such; their punishment, however, is beating.
Beating, binding, and likewise humiliating—this indeed is the punishment for a slave; a monetary fine is not ordained.
One who deserves death shall pay a fine of one hundred gold pieces;
for one deserving of mutilation, half of that; and for one deserving of exile, twenty-five.
According to the status of those who are noble, distinguished, or low-born,
he should confiscate their entire property and swiftly banish them from the city.
Those who are destitute should be placed in confinement; one must never carry out their execution.
According to the scriptures, this applies to all those guilty of crimes, with specific exceptions based on the nature of the offense.
A Brahmin deserving of execution or the amputation of limbs shall enter a prison free from restraints;
for once he is deprived of those acts, his conduct constitutes his true punishment.
One who gives false testimony should be banished after being publicly proclaimed; one who accepts gifts from the wicked should have his limbs severed;
and one who violates his own duty should be separated [from society] by means of imprisonment.
In those cases as well, one should prescribe the same for those who have committed equal offenses;
however, for children, the elderly, the sick, women, and the aged, there shall be no corporal punishment, but rather a fine as the penalty.
A righteous lord of the earth shall cause the woman's property to be given [to her] as a fine;
however, a woman who has committed an offense and is destitute deserves the punishment of a flogging.

One should deposit into the treasury wealth acquired by unjust means; for the sake of accomplishing a task, one might even cause the loss of that task, but a wise man should not bring it into the treasury.
Having given all that wealth arising from fines to the Brahmins,
and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should depart for the forest to lead the life of a renunciant.
Thus should the earthly king always act with diligence regarding his duties and for the welfare of the world; he should employ all his servants accordingly.
